examples.english: I accepted his proposal.
She rejected the invitation.

examples.korean: 우리는 새로운 조건을 받아들일지 고민 중이에요.
examples.english: We are thinking about whether to accept the new terms.

examples.english: He was angry and did not speak.
I calmly prepared before the exam.
When you are angry, take a deep breath.

These words are commonly used in daily conversations to agree or disagree with questions or requests. Understanding these antonyms helps beginners respond clearly in Korean.

examples.english: Can I buy this? Yes, please buy it.

examples.korean: 회의에 참석할 수 있나요? 아니요, 못 가요.
examples.english: Can you attend the meeting? No, I can't go.
Do you want to drink coffee? Yes, that sounds good.

These words are important when talking about travel or movement from one place to another. Knowing both helps you describe when someone comes to a place or goes away from it.

examples.english: A friend arrives at the house.
I leave for school.

examples.korean: 버스가 역에 오다 그리고 사람들이 가다.
examples.english: The bus arrives at the station and people leave.

pages.title: Ask vs Answer

These words are often used in conversations when people want to get or give information. Understanding these verbs helps you participate better in everyday Korean dialogues.

examples.english: Can I ask you a question?
The teacher answered the students.
My friend asked, and I answered.

examples.english: I attached the photo to the wall.
Please do not detach the sticker.
I attached the paper to the book and later detached it.

These phrases help you describe whether someone is currently awake or asleep. Understanding these opposites is useful for everyday conversations about sleep and daily activities.

examples.english: The child is awake now.
He was sleeping all night.
I am awake early in the morning.

'후' (hu) means 'after' and is used to describe something that happens later. These words help you talk about time order in everyday conversations.

examples.english: I prepare before the class.
I wash the dishes after the meal.
I stretch before and after exercise.

These words are opposites and are used to describe the size of objects, places, or people. Learning these antonyms helps you talk about size differences in everyday situations.

examples.english: This house is big.
That cat is small.
The bag is too big, so it's hard to carry.

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 빌리다 means 'to borrow,' which is when you take something from someone temporarily. 빌려주다 means 'to lend,' which is when you give something to someone for a short time. These two words are opposites and are used when talking about transferring items between people.

examples.english: I borrowed a book from my friend.
I lent a pencil to my younger sibling.

examples.korean: 필요하면 내 자전거를 빌릴 수 있어요.
examples.english: If you need it, you can borrow my bicycle.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows two opposite emotions in Korean: being brave and being scared. '용감한' means brave, describing someone who is not afraid. '무서운' means scared, describing someone who feels fear. Learning these words helps you talk about feelings clearly.

examples.english: He is a brave person.
I don't like scary movies.
The brave child climbed the tall mountain.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the antonyms 밝다 and 어둡다, which mean bright and dark in Korean. These words describe the amount of light in a place or object. 밝다 is used when something has a lot of light, and 어둡다 is used when something has little or no light. Learning these words helps you talk about lighting and colors in everyday situations.

examples.english: This room is bright, so it's good for studying.
At night, the street is dark, so you have to be careful.
The living room is very bright because the windows are big.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the difference between the Korean words 넓다 and 좁다. Both describe the size of a space or area. 넓다 means 'broad' or 'wide,' while 좁다 means 'slim' or 'narrow.' These words are often used to talk about rooms, streets, or other places.

examples.english: This room is broad, so it feels comfortable.

examples.korean: 이 길은 너무 좁아서 차가 못 다녀요.
examples.english: This street is too narrow, so cars cannot pass.

examples.korean: 우리 집 거실은 넓고 주방은 좁아요.
examples.english: Our living room is broad, and the kitchen is narrow.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows two opposite actions related to buildings and structures in Korean: 'Build' and 'Demolish.' 'Build' means to create or construct something new, while 'Demolish' means to tear down or destroy something that already exists. These words are often used when talking about houses, buildings, or other constructions.

examples.english: I want to build a new house.
They are demolishing an old building.

examples.korean: 회사는 공장을 짓고 나서 오래된 창고를 부셨어요.
examples.english: The company built a factory and then demolished the old warehouse.

examples.english: I am very busy today.
I am free tomorrow.
Please don't call me when I am busy.

These words are commonly used in everyday shopping and business situations. Learning both helps you understand basic transactions in Korean.

examples.english: I bought apples at the store.
That store sells clothes.
My friend sold me a book.

'깨끗한' means something is clean or tidy, while '더러운' means something is dirty or messy. Learning these opposites helps you talk about cleanliness in everyday situations.

examples.english: The room is in a clean state.
The shoes are dirty, so I need to wash them.
I wore clean clothes and went to school.

Understanding these antonyms helps you communicate clearly in everyday situations like entering or exiting rooms or buildings.

examples.english: Please open the door and come in.
Please go out when the meeting is over.
Guest, please come in! Be careful when you go out.

'수줍은' describes a person who feels shy or reserved around others. Learning these words helps you talk about different types of personalities.

examples.english: He is a confident person.
I feel shy in front of people I meet for the first time.
Having a confident attitude is important.

pages.title: Crowded vs Empty

examples.english: The subway station is always crowded in the morning.
The library is crowded during exam periods.
The streets are empty on Sunday nights.

These words describe the depth of objects like water, holes, or feelings. 깊다 means something is far down or has a lot of depth, while 얕다 means it is not deep or has little depth. Understanding these opposites helps you describe places and things more clearly.

examples.korean: 이 강은 너무 깊어서 수영하기 어려워요.
examples.english: This river is too deep, so it's hard to swim.

examples.korean: 저 호수는 얕아서 아이들이 놀기에 좋아요.
examples.english: That lake is shallow, so it's good for children to play.
That person's thoughts are deep and serious.

examples.english: My clothes got wet in the rain.
My hands are very dry.
The laundry will dry quickly.

examples.english: I went to school early.
I woke up late today.
Don't go to bed early and wake up late.

'늦은 밤' refers to late night, usually when people stay up very late. These words help describe different habits or times at night.

examples.english: I go to bed early at night.
I studied until late at night.
It is good to exercise early at night.

examples.english: This problem is easy.
Studying Korean is difficult.

examples.korean: 이 음식 만드는 법은 쉬워요, 하지만 맛있어요.
examples.english: The way to make this food is easy, but it is delicious.

examples.english: The refrigerator is empty.
The cup is full of water.
The bag is empty, so it is light.

examples.english: I enter the school.
I exit the house.
I entered the store and bought something.

examples.english: I am excited because the weather is nice today.
I am bored because the movie is not interesting.
I feel excited when I play with my friends.

Friend, thanks!
Thank you to my mother.

The bread is stale and cannot be eaten.
I bought fresh vegetables at the market.

There is a garden behind the house.
Please get on through the front door of the bus.

examples.english: The cup is full of water.
The refrigerator is empty.
The bag is full of books.

'배고프다' means you need to eat because you feel hungry. These words are useful for talking about your hunger and fullness in daily life.

examples.english: I am hungry now. Let's go eat.
I ate a lot, so I am full.
I eat snacks when I am hungry.

pages.title: Give vs Take

pages.intro: Need to remember the difference between give and take? Try this! 👇 🔴 주다 [juda] - to give
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the Korean verbs 주다 (juda) and 받다 (batda), which are opposites. 주다 means 'to give,' and 받다 means 'to take' or 'to receive.' These words are often used when talking about exchanging things between people. Learning both helps you understand how to talk about giving and receiving in Korean.

examples.english: I gave a book to my friend.
The teacher received the homework.
I want to receive a gift.

pages.title: Happy vs Sad

examples.english: I am really happy today.
I felt sad after watching that movie.

examples.korean: 행복할 때와 슬플 때의 기분은 달라요.
examples.english: The feelings when you are happy and sad are different.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows two opposite words related to health in Korean. '건강하다' means to be healthy, and '아프다' means to be sick. These words help you talk about how someone feels physically. Learning these antonyms is useful for everyday conversations about health.

examples.english: I am healthy right now.
I was sick yesterday, but I am okay today.
You need to exercise to be healthy.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the antonyms 'heavy' and 'light' in Korean. '무거워요' means something is heavy, and '가벼워요' means something is light. These words help describe the weight of objects in everyday situations. Learning these opposites is useful for comparing things.

examples.english: This bag is heavy.
That book is light.
I distinguish between heavy and light objects.

examples.english: This building is really high.
The desk is too low, so it's uncomfortable.
The mountain is high, and the sea is low.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the antonyms 'hot' and 'cold' in Korean. These words describe temperature and are often used to talk about weather, drinks, or feelings. Knowing these opposites helps you understand and express different temperature conditions easily.

examples.english: The weather is very hot today.
It is always cold in winter.

examples.korean: 이 물은 너무 차가워서 마시기 힘들어요.
examples.english: This water is too cold to drink.

pages.title: Include vs Exclude

pages.explanationEn: The words 포함하다 and 제외하다 are opposites in Korean. 포함하다 means to include something, while 제외하다 means to exclude or leave something out. These words are useful when talking about what is or isn't part of a group or list. Understanding these helps you describe what is included or excluded in different situations.

examples.english: This price includes tax.
We excluded a few people from the meeting.

examples.korean: 이 상품은 배송비가 포함되어 있지 않습니다.
examples.english: This product does not include shipping fees.

pages.title: Increase vs Decrease

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows two opposite words in Korean: 늘다 and 줄다. 늘다 means 'to increase' or 'to grow,' while 줄다 means 'to decrease' or 'to shrink.' These words are often used to talk about changes in numbers, amounts, or sizes. Learning these antonyms helps you describe how things change over time.

examples.english: The number of customers at our store has increased a lot.

examples.korean: 날씨가 추워지면 감기에 걸리는 사람이 줄어요.
examples.english: When the weather gets colder, the number of people catching a cold decreases.

examples.korean: 운동을 하면 체중이 줄 수 있어요.
examples.english: If you exercise, your weight can decrease.

pages.title: Indoor vs Outdoor

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the difference between indoor and outdoor places in Korean. "실내" means inside a building or room, while "실외" means outside or open air. These words are opposites and help describe where activities happen. Learning them helps you talk about locations clearly.

examples.english: We study indoors.
The weather was nice, so I exercised outdoors.

examples.korean: 실내와 실외 모두 마스크를 써야 해요.
examples.english: You have to wear a mask both indoors and outdoors.

examples.english: The book is inside the bag.
The cat is outside the house.

examples.korean: 우리는 방 안에 있고 친구들은 바깥에 있어요.
examples.english: We are inside the room, and our friends are outside.

pages.title: Kind vs Mean

These words describe how people treat others. Understanding these opposites helps you talk about people's behavior clearly.

examples.english: That teacher is always kind.
My younger sibling sometimes acts mean.
Kind people and mean people are different.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows two opposite actions related to airplanes: landing and taking off. '내리다' means to land, when the airplane comes down to the ground. '이륙하다' means to take off, when the airplane leaves the ground to fly. These words are useful when talking about travel and flights.

examples.english: The airplane will land soon.
The airplane has taken off.
We take off at 3 PM and land at 5 PM.

examples.english: Please go to the left.
There is a bank on the right.
Please distinguish well between left and right.

pages.title: Lend vs Borrow

examples.english: I lent a book to my friend.
I borrowed a book from the library.
Can you lend me a pencil?

pages.title: Light vs Dark

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the antonyms 밝다 and 어둡다, which describe brightness in Korean. 밝다 means 'light' or 'bright,' and 어둡다 means 'dark.' These words are often used to talk about the brightness of rooms, colors, or times of day. Learning these opposites helps you describe environments clearly.

examples.english: This room is bright, so it's good for studying.
At night, the road is dark, so you need to be careful.
Because the windows are big, the inside of the house is bright.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the Korean words for light and heavy. These words are opposites and describe the weight of objects. You can use them to talk about how heavy or light something feels. They are common adjectives in everyday conversation.

examples.english: This bag is light.
The book is too heavy.
Apples are light, and watermelons are heavy.

pages.title: Long vs Short

These words are opposites and are used to talk about the length of objects, time, or even hair. Understanding these words helps you describe things clearly in Korean.

examples.english: This clothes is too long.
My hair is short, so it feels cool.
If the class time is long, I get tired.

pages.title: Loud vs Quiet

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the opposite meanings of 'loud' and 'quiet' in Korean. '시끄럽다' means loud or noisy, and '조용하다' means quiet or calm. These words are often used to describe sounds or environments. Learning these antonyms helps you talk about different levels of noise.

examples.english: The library is always quiet.
This room is too loud.
You have to be quiet at school.

pages.title: Modern vs Traditional

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the difference between modern and traditional in Korean culture. '현대' means modern, referring to current or new styles and ideas. '전통' means traditional, referring to old customs and ways passed down through generations. Understanding these words helps you talk about changes in culture and lifestyle.

examples.english: Korean modern architecture is very cool.

examples.korean: 전통 음식은 오랜 역사를 가지고 있어요.
examples.english: Traditional food has a long history.

examples.korean: 현대 기술과 전통 문화가 함께 발전하고 있어요.
examples.english: Modern technology and traditional culture are developing together.

'더' is used when you want to say there is a greater amount, and '덜' is used when you want to say there is a smaller amount. They help you talk about differences in quantity clearly.

examples.english: I want to drink more coffee.
Today is less busy, so I like it.
I need a bigger bag.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the antonyms 'near' and 'far' in Korean. '가까워요' means something is close or near, while '멀어요' means something is distant or far away. These words are useful for talking about locations and distances in everyday situations.

examples.english: My house is near the school.
The store is far from my house.
Is the station near here?

pages.title: New vs Old (thing)

examples.english: This bag is new.
I like old things.
Please compare the new thing and the old thing.

pages.title: Noisy vs Silent

These words help you talk about places, people, or situations based on how loud or quiet they are. Learning these antonyms will improve your everyday Korean conversations.

examples.english: The library is always a quiet place.

I like that the house is quiet in the evening.

examples.english: Please give me some water.

Teacher, please give me the book.

These verbs are often used when talking about moving objects or opening doors. Understanding these words helps you describe basic physical actions clearly.

examples.english: I push the door to open it.
I pull the window to close it.
I push and pull the chair to change seats.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows two opposite words in Korean that describe being together or apart. '함께' means doing something with others or being together in the same place. '따로' means doing something separately or being apart. These words help you talk about relationships and how people or things are connected.

examples.english: We study together at school.
The friends went home separately.

examples.korean: 가족과 함께 시간을 보내는 것이 좋아요.
examples.english: I like spending time together with my family.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the Korean words for 'top' and 'bottom.' '위' means the upper part or top of something, while '아래' means the lower part or bottom. These words are often used to describe positions or locations. Learning these opposites helps you understand directions and places better in Korean.

examples.english: There is a book on top of the desk.
The cat is under the bed.

examples.korean: 그림의 위쪽과 아래쪽을 잘 봐야 해요.
examples.english: You need to look carefully at the top and bottom of the picture.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the Korean verbs for moving up and down. 올라가다 means to go up or ascend, and 내려가다 means to go down or descend. These words are often used when talking about stairs, hills, or any movement in a vertical direction. Learning these antonyms helps you describe directions clearly in Korean.

examples.english: I go up the stairs.
Please get off the bus.
I saw the scenery while going down the mountain.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the Korean words for 'upstream' and 'downstream,' which are opposites related to rivers. '상류' means the part of the river closer to its source, while '하류' means the part closer to where the river flows out. These words are useful when talking about directions or locations along a river.

examples.english: We fished upstream of the river.
There is a small village downstream.
It rained a lot, so the upstream area flooded.

pages.title: Warm vs Cool

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows two opposite words in Korean that describe temperature feelings: warm and cool. '따뜻하다' means warm, and '시원하다' means cool. These words are often used to talk about weather, drinks, or feelings. Learning these antonyms helps you describe different temperatures in everyday situations.

examples.english: The weather is warm today, so I feel good.
In summer, cool drinks are good.
This room is warm, but outside is cool.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the antonyms 넓다 and 좁다, which describe the width of something. 넓다 means 'wide' or 'spacious,' while 좁다 means 'narrow' or 'small in width.' These words are often used to talk about places, roads, rooms, and other spaces. Understanding these opposites helps you describe size and space clearly in Korean.

examples.korean: 이 방은 넓어서 친구들을 초대하기 좋아요.
examples.english: This room is wide, so it's good for inviting friends.

examples.korean: 이 골목은 너무 좁아서 차가 지나가기 힘들어요.
examples.english: This alley is too narrow, so it's hard for cars to pass.

examples.korean: 우리 집 앞마당이 넓고 꽃도 많아요.
examples.english: The front yard of our house is wide and has many flowers.

pages.intro: Feeling competitive today? Use these when you talk about games or sports 👇 🔴 이기다 [igida] - Win
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the Korean words for 'win' and 'lose,' which are antonyms used in competitions or games. '이기다' means to win or be victorious, and '지다' means to lose or be defeated. These words are commonly used in sports, games, and other competitive situations.

examples.english: Our team won the game.
I lost in soccer.
I want to win the competition.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the opposite words for age in Korean: young and old. '어리다' means to be young, and '늙다' means to be old. These words help describe how old someone or something is. Learning these antonyms is useful for talking about people or animals at different ages.

examples.korean: 나는 어릴 때 친구들과 많이 놀았어요.
examples.english: I played a lot with friends when I was young.
Grandfather has gotten very old.
Puppies are really cute when they are young.

This is an example of a compound word where the meanings of the two parts come together to describe a specific body part.

examples.english: Be careful with your ankle when exercising.
He injured his ankle, so it's hard to walk.
If you have pain in your ankle, go to the hospital.

pages.title: 밤 + 하늘 = 밤하늘
pages.description: This chart shows how two Korean words combine to form a new compound word. '밤' means 'night' and '하늘' means 'sky.' When combined, they create '밤하늘,' which me…

pages.intro: Handy Korean for 밤 + 하늘 = 밤하늘 ✨ 🔴 밤 [bam] - Night
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how two Korean words combine to form a new compound word. '밤' means 'night' and '하늘' means 'sky.' When combined, they create '밤하늘,' which means 'night sky.' This is a common way to make new words in Korean by blending two related words together.

examples.english: There are many stars in the night sky.
We talked while looking at the night sky.
The night sky is really beautiful.

pages.title: 불 + 고기 = 불고기
pages.description: This chart shows how two Korean words combine to form a new word. '불' means 'fire' and '고기' means 'meat.' When combined, they create '불고기,' which is a popula…

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how two Korean words combine to form a new word. '불' means 'fire' and '고기' means 'meat.' When combined, they create '불고기,' which is a popular Korean dish made by grilling marinated meat over fire. This is an example of a compound word where the meaning comes from both parts together.

examples.english: I ate bulgogi for dinner.
Bulgogi is a famous food in Korea.
Grilling bulgogi over fire makes it delicious.

pages.title: 별 + 빛 = 별빛

pages.explanationEn: The compound word '별빛' is made by combining '별' (star) and '빛' (light). It means 'starlight,' which is the light that comes from stars. This type of word formation is common in Korean, where two simple words are joined to create a new meaning. Learning compound words helps you understand how Korean builds vocabulary.

examples.english: The starlight is twinkling in the night sky.
I took a walk under the starlight.
The starlight is very beautiful.

pages.title: 책 + 방 = 책방
pages.description: The word '책방' is a compound word made by combining '책' (book) and '방' (room). Together, they form '책방,' which means 'bookstore' or 'bookshop' in Korean. This…

pages.intro: Handy Korean for 책 + 방 = 책방 ✨ 🔴 책 [chaek] - Book
pages.explanationEn: The word '책방' is a compound word made by combining '책' (book) and '방' (room). Together, they form '책방,' which means 'bookstore' or 'bookshop' in Korean. This shows how two simple words can blend to create a new meaning. Compound words like this are common in Korean vocabulary and help learners understand how words connect.

examples.korean: 나는 주말에 책방에 가서 책을 샀어요.
examples.english: I went to the bookstore on the weekend and bought a book.
There is a small bookstore in our neighborhood.
I found a new novel at the bookstore.

pages.title: 책 + 상 = 책상

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how two Korean words combine to form a new compound word. The word '책' means 'book' and '상' means 'table.' When combined, they create '책상,' which means 'desk' or 'study table.' This is a common way to form new words in Korean by blending meanings.

examples.english: There is a book on the desk.
I bought a new desk.
I study at the desk.

pages.title: 달 + 빛 = 달빛

pages.intro: Handy Korean for 달 + 빛 = 달빛 ✨ 🔴 달 [dal] - Moon
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how two Korean words combine to form a new compound word. The word '달빛' is made by blending '달' meaning 'moon' and '빛' meaning 'light.' Together, they create the word for 'moonlight.' This is a common way in Korean to form new vocabulary by joining two meaningful words.

examples.english: The moonlight is very bright at night.
I took a walk under the moonlight.
Moonlight comes through the window.

pages.title: 해 + 빛 = 햇빛
pages.description: The compound word '햇빛' is formed by combining '해' meaning 'sun' and '빛' meaning 'light.' Together, they describe the sunlight or the light that comes from th…

pages.explanationEn: The compound word '햇빛' is formed by combining '해' meaning 'sun' and '빛' meaning 'light.' Together, they describe the sunlight or the light that comes from the sun. This type of compound word blends two simple words to create a new meaning related to nature and daily life. Understanding such compounds helps learners recognize how Korean builds new vocabulary.

examples.english: Sunlight comes in through the window.
The sunlight is so strong that I wear sunglasses.
I take a walk in the morning while enjoying the sunlight.

pages.title: 입 + 맛 = 입맛

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how two Korean words combine to form a new word with a related meaning. The word '입' means 'mouth' and '맛' means 'taste.' When combined as '입맛,' it refers to one's appetite or taste preference. This is an example of a compound word where the meaning is created by blending the original words.

examples.english: I have no appetite today.
I like spicy food, so my appetite is stimulated.

examples.korean: 새로운 음식을 먹으면 입맛이 바뀔 수 있어요.
examples.english: Eating new food can change your taste preference.

pages.title: 입 + 술 = 입술
pages.description: The word '입술' is a compound word made by combining '입' (mouth) and '술' (lip). This type of word formation is common in Korean, where two words join to create…
pages.imageAlt: 입 + 술 = 입술 in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for 입 + 술 = 입술 ✨ 🔴 입 [ip] - Mouth
pages.explanationEn: The word '입술' is a compound word made by combining '입' (mouth) and '술' (lip). This type of word formation is common in Korean, where two words join to create a new meaning related to both parts. '입술' specifically refers to the lips, an important part of the mouth used for speaking and eating. Understanding compound words like this helps learners expand their vocabulary efficiently.

examples.english: Her lips are red.
I applied lip balm on my lips.
My lips were dry, so I drank water.

pages.title: 꽃 + 병 = 꽃병

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how two Korean words, 꽃 (flower) and 병 (vase or bottle), combine to form a new compound word 꽃병, which means flower vase. In Korean, many compound words are created by joining two nouns to express a new meaning related to both original words. Understanding these combinations helps learners expand their vocabulary and recognize word patterns.

examples.english: I put pretty flowers in the vase.
The flower vase is on the table.
Flower and vase came together to become a flower vase.

pages.title: 물 + 개 = 물개
pages.description: This chart shows a compound word made by combining two Korean words: 물 (water) and 개 (dog). The new word 물개 means 'seal,' an animal that lives both in water…

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows a compound word made by combining two Korean words: 물 (water) and 개 (dog). The new word 물개 means 'seal,' an animal that lives both in water and on land. Compound words like this are common in Korean and help describe new ideas by blending simple words.

examples.english: Seals live in the sea.
I saw a seal at the zoo.
The seal swims in the water.

pages.title: 눈 + 물 = 눈물
pages.description: The compound word 눈물 combines 눈 (eye) and 물 (water) to mean tears. This shows how two simple words can blend to create a new word with a related meaning. Und…
pages.imageAlt: 눈 + 물 = 눈물 in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for 눈 + 물 = 눈물 ✨ 🔴 눈 [nun] - Eye
pages.explanationEn: The compound word 눈물 combines 눈 (eye) and 물 (water) to mean tears. This shows how two simple words can blend to create a new word with a related meaning. Understanding such compound words helps learners connect vocabulary and recognize patterns in Korean. 눈물 is a common word used to describe the water that comes from your eyes when you cry or feel emotional.

examples.english: She was moved and tears came out.
I had tears, so I looked for a tissue.
The baby cried and tears flowed.

pages.intro: Handy Korean for 눈 + 사람 = 눈사람 ✨ 🔴 눈 [nun] - Snow
pages.explanationEn: The compound word '눈사람' combines '눈' meaning 'snow' and '사람' meaning 'person.' This type of word blend creates a new word that describes a snowman. In Korean, many compound words are formed by joining two simple words to express a new idea or object.

examples.korean: 어제 눈이 많이 와서 눈사람을 만들었어요.
examples.english: It snowed a lot yesterday, so I made a snowman.

examples.korean: 아이들이 공원에서 눈사람을 즐겁게 만들고 있어요.
examples.english: The children are happily making snowmen in the park.

examples.korean: 눈사람은 겨울에만 볼 수 있는 재미있는 모양이에요.
examples.english: A snowman is a fun shape that you can only see in winter.

pages.title: 신 + 발 = 신발

pages.intro: Handy Korean for 신 + 발 = 신발 ✨ 🔴 신 [sin] - Shoe (bound form)
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how two Korean words combine to form a new compound word. The word 신 (shin) means "to wear" or "put on," and 발 (bal) means "foot." When combined, 신발 (sinbal) means "shoes." This is a common way Korean forms new words by blending two related words.

examples.english: I bought new shoes.
The shoes are too small.
I wear shoes when I go to school.

pages.title: 손 + 목 = 손목
pages.description: This chart shows how two Korean words combine to form a new word. "손" means "hand" and "목" means "neck". When combined, they create "손목," which means "wrist.…

pages.intro: Handy Korean for 손 + 목 = 손목 ✨ 🔴 손 [son] - Hand
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how two Korean words combine to form a new word. "손" means "hand" and "목" means "neck". When combined, they create "손목," which means "wrist." This is an example of a compound word where the meaning relates to a part of the body connecting the hand and arm.

examples.english: Be careful with your wrist when exercising.
I am wearing a wristwatch.
My wrist hurt, so I went to the hospital.

pages.title: 손 + 톱 = 손톱
pages.description: The compound word 손톱 is made by combining 손 (hand) and 톱 (nail). It refers to the fingernail or toenail on your hand or foot. This shows how Korean forms new…

pages.intro: Handy Korean for 손 + 톱 = 손톱 ✨ 🔴 손 [son] - Hand
pages.explanationEn: The compound word 손톱 is made by combining 손 (hand) and 톱 (nail). It refers to the fingernail or toenail on your hand or foot. This shows how Korean forms new words by blending two simple words to create a specific meaning. Understanding these compounds helps learners expand their vocabulary quickly.

examples.english: I cut my fingernails.
My fingernails are long, so it's uncomfortable.
I applied nail polish on my fingernails.

pages.title: 술 + 고래 = 술고래
pages.description: The word '술고래' is a compound word made by combining '술' (alcohol) and '고래' (whale). It is a playful term used to describe someone who drinks a lot, similar t…
pages.imageAlt: 술 + 고래 = 술고래 in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for 술 + 고래 = 술고래 ✨ 🔴 술 [sul] - Alcohol
pages.explanationEn: The word '술고래' is a compound word made by combining '술' (alcohol) and '고래' (whale). It is a playful term used to describe someone who drinks a lot, similar to how a whale consumes a large amount of water. This word is often used in casual conversations to talk about heavy drinkers in a friendly way.

examples.korean: 우리 형은 술고래라서 술자리에서 항상 끝까지 있어요.
examples.english: My older brother is a heavy drinker, so he always stays until the end at drinking parties.

examples.korean: 술고래 친구 때문에 술 마시는 게 힘들어요.
examples.english: Drinking is hard because of my friend who drinks a lot.
He is a heavy drinker but takes good care of his health.

pages.imageAlt: This vs that feel in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Confused about "this," "that," and "that over there" in Korean? 🔴 이것 [igeot] - this (near me)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, words like 이것, 그것, and 저것 are used to point out things based on their location. 이것 means 'this' for something near the speaker, 그것 means 'that' for something near the listener, and 저것 means 'that' for something far from both. 어느 것 means 'which one?' and is used when asking to choose between options.

examples.english: This is my book.
That is your bag.
What is that over there?

pages.title: Already vs yet in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 이미 and 벌써 both mean "already," but 벌써 is used when something happened sooner than expected or with surprise. 아직 means "not yet," indicating someth…
pages.imageAlt: Already vs yet in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Confused about "already" vs "yet" in Korean? 🔴 이미 [imi] - already (fact)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 이미 and 벌써 both mean "already," but 벌써 is used when something happened sooner than expected or with surprise. 아직 means "not yet," indicating something has not happened up to now. 아직도 means "still," showing that something continues to happen or remain the same. These words help express time and expectations clearly in daily conversations.

examples.english: I already did my homework.
Did you already have dinner? (with surprise)
I haven't done my homework yet.

pages.title: Already / yet / still in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 'already,' 'yet,' and 'still' are expressed with different words that show time and completion. '벌써' means 'already' and shows something happened…
pages.imageAlt: Already / yet / still in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How to say "already," "yet," and "still" in Korean when talking about time? 🔴 벌써 [beolsseo] - already
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 'already,' 'yet,' and 'still' are expressed with different words that show time and completion. '벌써' means 'already' and shows something happened sooner than expected. '아직 안' means 'not yet' and is used to say something hasn't happened but is expected. '아직' means 'still' and shows something is continuing. '더 이상' means 'anymore' and is used to say something no longer happens.

examples.english: I already finished my homework.
I haven't eaten yet.
He is still at home.

pages.title: Asking politely in Korean

Where is the bathroom?

pages.title: Because & so in Korean
pages.description: Because and so are common connectors in Korean used to explain reasons and results. 왜냐하면 means "because" and introduces a reason. 그래서 and 그러니까 both mean "so"…
pages.imageAlt: Because & so in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Learn how to connect ideas in Korean with these handy words 👇 🔴 왜냐하면 [waenyahamyeon] - because
pages.explanationEn: Because and so are common connectors in Korean used to explain reasons and results. 왜냐하면 means "because" and introduces a reason. 그래서 and 그러니까 both mean "so" or "therefore" and show the result or conclusion. 그래서요 is a casual way to say "that's why" in conversation.

examples.english: It is raining. So, I am staying at home.
Because I was hungry, I ate food.
I'm late. So, I have to go quickly.

pages.title: Because / so scenes in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows Korean words used to explain reasons and results. '왜냐하면' means 'because' and is used to give a reason. '그래서' means 'so' or 'therefore' and s…
pages.imageAlt: Because / so scenes in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Want to explain reasons in Korean? 🔴 왜냐하면 [waenyahamyeon] - because
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows Korean words used to explain reasons and results. '왜냐하면' means 'because' and is used to give a reason. '그래서' means 'so' or 'therefore' and shows the result. '그래서요' is a casual way to say 'that's why.' '그 이유로' means 'for that reason' and is more formal.

examples.korean: 나는 배고파요 왜냐하면 아침을 안 먹었어요.
examples.english: I am hungry because I didn't eat breakfast.
It rained, so I stayed at home.

examples.korean: 오늘은 피곤해요. 그래서요, 일찍 잘 거예요.
examples.english: I am tired today. That's why I will sleep early.

pages.title: Become / change in Korean

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows Korean verbs related to becoming or changing. '되다' means to become or to turn into something. '바꾸다' is used when you change something else, like an object or a plan. '변하다' describes a change in yourself or something's state. These verbs help you talk about changes in everyday life.

examples.english: I want to become a doctor.
I changed the color of my clothes.
The weather has changed a lot.

pages.title: Before / after / while in Korean

pages.imageAlt: Before / after / while in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Learn to talk about time in Korean! Use these when you want to say before, after, or while. 🔴 전에 [jeone] - before
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, '전에', '후에', '면서', and '자마자' are used to talk about the timing of actions. '전에' means 'before' and is used to describe something that happens earlier. '후에' means 'after' and shows that one action happens later. '면서' means 'while' and is used when two actions happen at the same time. '자마자' means 'as soon as' and indicates that one action happens immediately after another.

examples.korean: 저는 학교에 가기 전에 아침을 먹어요.
examples.english: I eat breakfast before going to school.
I will meet my friend after class.
I do my homework while listening to music.

pages.title: Before & after timing in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows common Korean words used to talk about time in relation to events: before, after, and during. '전에' means 'before' something happens, and '후에…
pages.imageAlt: Before & after timing in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for before & after timing ✨ 🔴 전에 [jeone] - before
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean words used to talk about time in relation to events: before, after, and during. '전에' means 'before' something happens, and '후에' means 'after' something happens. '동안' is used to express 'during' a period of time, while '그동안' refers to 'meanwhile' or 'in the meantime' between events.

examples.english: I do my homework before class.
I take a walk after dinner.

examples.korean: 영화를 보는 동안 조용히 해 주세요.
examples.english: Please be quiet during the movie.

pages.title: Before vs after in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 'before' and 'after' are used to talk about when something happens in relation to another event. '전에' means 'before' and is used after a noun or v…

pages.intro: How to say BEFORE and AFTER in Korean? Use these when you talk about time! 👇 🔴 수업 전에 [sueop jeone] - before class
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 'before' and 'after' are used to talk about when something happens in relation to another event. '전에' means 'before' and is used after a noun or verb to show something happens earlier. '후에' means 'after' and is used similarly to show something happens later. These expressions help describe time order clearly.

examples.english: I do my homework before class.
I meet my friend after class.
Please wash your hands before eating.

pages.title: Begin vs end in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows Korean words related to beginning and ending actions. '시작' means to begin, and '끝' means to end. You can also use '일시정지' to pause something…

pages.intro: Want to say "begin" and "end" in Korean? 👇 🔴 시작 [sijak] - begin
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows Korean words related to beginning and ending actions. '시작' means to begin, and '끝' means to end. You can also use '일시정지' to pause something temporarily, and '다시 시작' to resume or start again. These words help describe the order of events or activities.

examples.english: The class has begun.
The movie has ended.
I will pause briefly and then resume.

pages.title: Big vs small in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows how to talk about size and quantity in Korean using common adjectives. '커요' means big, and '작아요' means small. For quantity, '많아요' means many…
pages.imageAlt: Big vs small in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Big or small? Let's see how Koreans say it! 🔴 커요 [keoyo] - big
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how to talk about size and quantity in Korean using common adjectives. '커요' means big, and '작아요' means small. For quantity, '많아요' means many, and '적어요' means few. These words help you describe objects and amounts in everyday conversations.

examples.english: This bag is big.
There are many apples.
There are few books.

pages.intro: Need to borrow or lend something in Korean? Use these words in real life 👇 🔴 빌려요 [billyeoyo] - Borrow
pages.explanationEn: These Korean verbs are used when talking about borrowing, lending, returning, and keeping things. 빌려요 means to borrow something from someone. 빌려줘요 means to lend something to someone. 돌려줘요 means to return something to its owner. 가져요 means to keep or have something with you.

examples.english: I borrow a book from my friend.
I lend a pencil to my younger sibling.
After reading the book, I return it to my friend.

pages.title: Can vs can't scenes in Korean
pages.titleEn: Can vs can't scenes in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows how to express ability and inability in Korean using different tenses. '할 수 있어요' means 'I can,' showing present ability. '못해요' means 'I can'…

pages.intro: Can or can't? Let's see how to say it in Korean in real situations👇 🔴 할 수 있어요 [hal su isseoyo] - I can
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how to express ability and inability in Korean using different tenses. '할 수 있어요' means 'I can,' showing present ability. '못해요' means 'I can't,' indicating present inability. For past actions, '할 수 있었어요' means 'I was able to,' and '못했어요' means 'I couldn't.' These phrases help you talk about what you can or cannot do now and in the past.

examples.english: I can speak Korean.
I couldn't do my homework yesterday.

examples.korean: 그는 어제 운동을 할 수 있었어요.
examples.english: He was able to exercise yesterday.

pages.title: Can vs may nuance in Korean
pages.titleEn: Can vs may nuance in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 'can' and 'may' express ability and permission, but they have different nuances. '할 수 있어요' shows you have the ability to do something. '해도 돼요' mea…
pages.imageAlt: Can vs may nuance in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Can vs May in Korean? Here's the quick difference: 🔴 할 수 있어요 [hal su isseoyo] - I can do it (ability)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 'can' and 'may' express ability and permission, but they have different nuances. '할 수 있어요' shows you have the ability to do something. '해도 돼요' means you have permission to do it. Negative forms like '못 해요' and '하면 안 돼요' express inability and prohibition, respectively.

examples.english: I can speak Korean.
May I take pictures here?
You shouldn't use your phone now.

pages.title: Clean vs dirty in Korean

pages.intro: Clean or dirty? Learn these easy words to describe your room or clothes👇 🔴 깨끗해요 [kkaekkeuthaeyo] - clean
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean words to describe cleanliness and tidiness. You can use 깨끗해요 to say something is clean and 더러워요 to say it is dirty. 정리됐어요 means that something is tidy or organized, while 지저분해요 means it is messy or cluttered. These words help you talk about the state of a room or objects at home.

examples.english: The room is clean.
The desk is dirty.
The closet is tidy.
The living room is messy.

pages.title: Come vs go in Korean

The verbs '들어와요' and '나가요' add more detail by specifying 'come in' and 'go out.' Understanding these verbs helps with basic motion and direction in Korean conversations.

examples.english: I go to school.
A friend comes to my house.
Open the door and come in.

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, different counters are used to count people, animals, books, and general objects. For example, '명' is used for people, '마리' for animals, '권' for books, and '개' for things. These counters come after numbers to specify what you are counting. Learning these counters helps you speak more naturally and clearly in Korean.

examples.english: Two friends went to school.
I bought two apples.

examples.korean: 강아지 두 마리가 공원에서 놀고 있어요.
examples.english: Two puppies are playing in the park.

pages.title: This that these those in Korean
pages.titleEn: This that these those in Korean

pages.intro: Learn how to say this, that, and those in Korean — super useful for pointing things out! 👇 🔴 이것 [igeot] - this
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, demonstratives like 이것, 그것, 저것, and 이것들 help you point to things based on their location. 이것 means 'this' for something close to the speaker. 그것 means 'that' for something near the listener. 저것 refers to 'that' over there, far from both. 이것들 is the plural form of 이것, meaning 'these'.

examples.english: This is my book.
That is your bag.
Those over there are mountains.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows words used to talk about arriving early, on time, or late in Korean. You can use these words to describe when someone gets somewhere compared to the expected time. It helps you understand how to talk about time and punctuality in everyday situations.

examples.english: I always go to school early.
The bus arrived on time.
I was too late for the meeting. I'm sorry.

'제시간에' is used when something happens exactly on time. '지연' refers to a delay or something happening later than expected.

examples.english: I always go to school early.
The meeting started on time.
The plane was delayed, so it arrived late.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows pairs of Korean adjectives that describe how easy or hard something is, and how comfortable or uncomfortable it feels. 쉬워요 means 'easy' and 어려워요 means 'hard.' 편해요 means 'comfortable' and 불편해요 means 'uncomfortable.' These words help you talk about your feelings or experiences with tasks, places, or things.

examples.english: This problem is easy.
This homework is hard.
This chair is comfortable.

pages.title: Fast vs slow in Korean

pages.intro: Need to talk about speed in Korean? Use these handy phrases! 🔴 빨라요 [ppallayo] - fast
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how to talk about speed in Korean. You can say 빨라요 to mean something is fast and 느려요 to say it is slow. To tell someone to hurry, use 서두르세요, and to ask someone to take their time, say 천천히 하세요. These phrases help you describe and ask about how fast or slow things happen.

examples.english: The bus is fast.
The computer is slow.
Hurry up! There is no time.

pages.title: First / last / next in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows common Korean words used to talk about order and sequence. '먼저' means 'first' and is used when something happens before others. '마지막' means…

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean words used to talk about order and sequence. '먼저' means 'first' and is used when something happens before others. '마지막' means 'last' and refers to the final item or event. '다음' means 'next' and points to what comes after. '이전' means 'previous' and refers to what came before. These words help you describe the order of events or things in everyday conversation.

examples.english: Wash your hands first.
I missed the last bus.
I will get off at the next station.

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean words used to describe how full or empty something is. You can say 가득해요 when something is full, 비었어요 when it is empty, 반 for half, and 넘쳐요 when it overflows. These words help you talk about quantity and space in everyday situations.

examples.english: The cup is full.
The refrigerator is empty.
The water bottle is half full.

The phrases '해 주세요' and '해 줄게요' are polite ways to ask for or offer help, meaning 'please do for me' and 'I'll do it for you,' respectively. These words are useful for everyday conversations when exchanging things or favors.

examples.english: My friend gave me a gift.
I received a letter.
Please help me. The homework is difficult.

examples.english: My friend gives me a book.
I receive a letter.
The teacher returns the test papers.

pages.title: Give vs receive in Korean

You can use polite forms like '주세요' to ask someone to give you something, and past tense like '받았어요' to say you received something. These verbs are essential for everyday conversations in Korean.

examples.english: Please give me the book.
I received a gift.
My friend gave me food.

examples.english: I am really happy today.
I feel sad after watching the movie.
I am angry because my friend is late.

pages.title: Have to vs want to in Korean
pages.titleEn: Have to vs want to in Korean

pages.intro: Mixing up "have to" and "want to" in Korean? 👀 🔴 해야 해요 [haeya haeyo] - I have to
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 'have to' and 'want to' show different feelings about doing something. '해야 해요' means you must do something, showing obligation. '하고 싶어요' means you want to do something, showing desire. There are also ways to say you don't have to do something or shouldn't do something.

examples.english: I have to do homework today.
I want to watch a movie.
You shouldn't smoke here.

pages.title: Hear vs listen in Korean

The negative form '안 들려요' means 'can't hear,' and '잘 들어요' means 'listen carefully.' These verbs help express how you perceive or focus on sounds.

examples.english: I can hear music from outside.
I listen carefully to the teacher.
It's quiet, so I can't hear any sound.

examples.english: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.
I wish to learn Korean.
I hope everyone stays healthy.

These words help you talk about how food and drinks feel and taste.

examples.english: This soup is hot. Please be careful.
I like cold drinks.
This food is spicy, but sweet.

examples.english: I am hungry. I want to eat rice.

examples.english: If it rains, I stay at home.
I meet my friend when I go to school.
I do my homework after eating.

These pronouns help talk about people without specifying exactly who they are. They are useful in everyday conversation when the exact person is not important or unknown.

examples.english: Everybody went to school.
Somebody is at the door.
Nobody knows that story.

examples.english: The book is inside the bag.
The cat is outside the house.
Please sit inside here.

pages.title: Invite & soft refuse

examples.english: Friend, do you want to come watch a movie?
Sure! Let's go together.
I can't today. Maybe next time.

You can use these phrases in everyday conversations when making plans with friends or colleagues. Understanding these helps you communicate politely and clearly in social situations.

examples.english: I invite my friend.
Thank you for the invitation. I will go.
This time is difficult. Let's do it next time.

To say you know how to do something, use '할 줄 알아요.' When you want to say you have learned something, use '배웠어요.' These phrases are common in everyday conversations.

examples.english: I know Korean.
I don't know this problem.
I know how to play the piano.

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 'know' and 'think' are expressed with different verbs that show how sure or unsure you are about something. '알아요' means you know something for sure, while '몰라요' means you don't know. '생각해요' is used when you think or have an opinion, and '추측해요' means you guess or make a guess based on some information. These words help express different levels of certainty and thought.

examples.english: I know that person.
I think the weather will be good today.
I don't know the answer. I'm just guessing.

When you give something back, you use '돌려주다'. '잠깐 쓸게' is a casual phrase to say you will keep something for a short time.

examples.english: Can I borrow the book?
I will lend you a pencil.
I will return the book tomorrow.

'빌려줘요' means to lend something to someone. '돌려줘요' means to return something to someone. '가져요' means to keep or have something. These verbs help you talk about sharing and exchanging items in everyday situations.

examples.english: I borrow a book.
I lend money to my friend.
I return the pencil.

pages.title: Like love hate in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows common Korean verbs used to express feelings like liking, loving, disliking, and hating something or someone. These verbs are often used in…

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean verbs used to express feelings like liking, loving, disliking, and hating something or someone. These verbs are often used in everyday conversations to share your emotions clearly. They all end with 해요, which is a polite way to speak. Learning these words helps you talk about your preferences and feelings naturally.

examples.english: I like chocolate.
She loves her family.
I dislike spicy food.

examples.english: I like coffee.
I prefer coffee to tea.
I love my family.

pages.title: Listen vs hear scenes

pages.intro: Listen vs Hear in real life 👂 🔴 듣다 [deutda] - actively listen
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 듣다 means to listen actively, focusing on sounds or speech. 들리다 means to hear something that is audible, often without trying. 우연히 듣다 means to overhear by chance, and 못 들은 척 means to pretend not to hear or ignore sounds. These words help describe different ways of perceiving sound in everyday situations.

examples.english: I am listening to music.
I can hear children laughing outside.

examples.korean: 그는 내 이야기를 못 들은 척했어요.
examples.english: He pretended not to hear my story.

pages.explanationEn: Location particles in Korean show where an action happens or the direction of movement. '에' indicates a destination or place where something exists. '에서' is used to show the place where an action takes place. '으로' points to a direction or means by which something is done. '부터' marks the starting point in time or place.

examples.english: I go to school.
I study at the library.
I came home by bus.

examples.english: I drink more water.
This food is less spicy.

examples.korean: 그 가게가 가장 싼 가격을 가지고 있어요.

examples.english: I study more than my friend.
This bag is the most beautiful.
Today is less cold than yesterday.

pages.title: Must vs should in Korean

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 'must' and 'should' express different levels of obligation or advice. '해야 해요' means you have to do something, showing a strong necessity. '하는 게 좋아요' suggests that it is better or advisable to do something, but it is not mandatory. There are also expressions like '안 해도 돼요' meaning you don't have to do something, and '하는 편이 좋아요' which means it is better to do something, often used for polite advice.

examples.english: You must do your homework.
You should exercise.
You don't have to do it today.

pages.title: Must / should / can in Korean

examples.english: I must do my homework.
You should go to bed early.
I can speak Korean.

pages.title: Must / should / may in Korean

'하는 게 좋아요' means 'should' and suggests a good idea or recommendation. '해도 돼요' means 'may' or 'allowed,' giving permission. '하면 안 돼요' means 'must not' and tells you something is not allowed.

examples.english: You must do your homework.
You should exercise.
You may take pictures here.

pages.title: Must / should modality in Korean

'하는 게 좋아요' suggests you should do something, meaning it is recommended. '안 해도 돼요' means you don't have to do something, so it is optional. '하면 안 돼요' means you must not do something, indicating prohibition.

examples.english: You must do your homework.
You should exercise.
You don't have to sleep late.

pages.title: Near vs far in Korean

You can also use '옆에' to say 'next to' and '건너편에' to say 'across from' something. These words help describe where things are in relation to each other.

examples.english: My house is next to the school.
The store is near my house.
The bank is across the street, and the library is far.

pages.title: Open/close vs on/off

examples.english: I opened the door and entered the room.
Please turn on the light.
I closed the window and turned off the light.

Understanding these pairs helps you describe actions clearly.

examples.english: I open the door.
I turn on the light.
I close the window.

pages.title: Please vs want in Korean

'갖고 싶어요' and '하고 싶어요' express desires to have or do something. '해도 돼요?' is a polite way to ask for permission. These phrases help you make requests, express wishes, and ask for approval in everyday conversations.

examples.english: Please give me some water.
I want a new bag.
May I take a picture here?

examples.english: Hello! How are you feeling today?
Hi! Have you been well?
Thank you. I appreciate your help.

pages.title: Possible vs impossible in Korean

pages.explanationEn: This chart shows words used to express possibility and certainty in Korean. '가능해요' means something is possible, while '불가능해요' means it is impossible. '아마' is used to say 'maybe' when you are not sure. '분명히' means 'definitely' or with certainty.

examples.english: This task is possible.
That plan is impossible.
Maybe it will rain tomorrow.
You will definitely pass the exam.

examples.english: I put the book on the desk.
I take the umbrella home.
I take the phone out of the bag.

pages.title: Remember vs forget

I almost forgot. Please remind me.

You will see words for 'remember,' 'forget,' and useful phrases to ask someone to remind you or tell someone not to forget. These expressions are common in daily conversations and important for beginners to understand and use.

examples.english: I remember the meeting time tomorrow.
I forgot my keys.
Don't forget the important appointment.

examples.english: This answer is right.

It is almost exactly right.

pages.title: Same vs different in Korean

These words are useful for everyday conversations when you want to talk about comparisons and accuracy.

examples.english: Our thoughts are the same.
These two bags are different.
These pictures are similar.
