pages.imageAlt: See / watch / look scenes in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How do you say "see" or "watch" in Korean? It depends on the situation! 👀 보다 [boda] - to look at something quickly
pages.explanationEn: These Korean verbs all relate to seeing or watching, but they have different meanings. 보다 means to look at something briefly or generally. 지켜보다 means to watch something carefully for a while. 구경하다 means to sightsee or look around a place. 쳐다보다 means to stare at something, often with focus or surprise.

examples.english: I am looking out the window.

examples.korean: 아이가 놀이터에서 노는 것을 지켜보고 있어요.
examples.english: I am watching the child playing at the playground.
I sightsee famous places in Seoul.

pages.title: Seem / feel / look in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, words like 것 같아요, 느껴져요, 보여요, and 들려요 are used to express how something seems, feels, looks, or sounds. These expressions help you share your impre…
pages.imageAlt: Seem / feel / look in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How to say "seem," "feel," and "look" in Korean? 🤔 Use these when describing things around you👇
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, words like 것 같아요, 느껴져요, 보여요, and 들려요 are used to express how something seems, feels, looks, or sounds. These expressions help you share your impressions or guesses about a situation or object. They are often used in everyday conversations to describe your thoughts or feelings based on what you observe or sense.

examples.english: It seems like the weather is good today.

examples.korean: 이 음악이 정말 기분 좋게 느껴져요.
examples.english: This music really feels good.
That flower looks pretty.

pages.title: Seems / looks like in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, expressions like '것 같아요', '보여요', '들려요', and '느낌이 들어요' are used to say something seems or looks a certain way. They help you share your guesses or…
pages.imageAlt: Seems / looks like in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How do you say "seems like" or "looks like" in Korean? 🔴 것 같아요 [geot gatayo] - seems like
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, expressions like '것 같아요', '보여요', '들려요', and '느낌이 들어요' are used to say something seems or looks a certain way. They help you share your guesses or feelings about what you see, hear, or sense. These phrases are useful for polite conversation when you want to express uncertainty or make a soft statement.

examples.english: It seems like the weather will be good today.
That person looks happy.
I hear the sound of the door closing.

pages.title: Self vs others in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows words used to talk about doing things by yourself or with others in Korean. '스스로' means doing something by yourself, while '서로' means doing…
pages.imageAlt: Self vs others in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Know the difference between self and others in Korean👇 🔴 스스로 [seuseuro] - by myself
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows words used to talk about doing things by yourself or with others in Korean. '스스로' means doing something by yourself, while '서로' means doing something with each other. '혼자' means alone, and '같이' means together. These words help you describe who is involved in an action.

examples.english: I study by myself.
We help each other.
I watch a movie together with a friend.

pages.title: Speak vs say in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 말해요 (malhaeyo) means 'say' and is used when quoting or expressing specific words. 이야기해요 (iyagihaeyo) means 'speak' or 'talk' and is used for gener…
pages.imageAlt: Speak vs say in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Speak vs say in Korean: when to use 말해요 or 이야기해요? 🔴 말해요 [malhaeyo] - say (a specific thing)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 말해요 (malhaeyo) means 'say' and is used when quoting or expressing specific words. 이야기해요 (iyagihaeyo) means 'speak' or 'talk' and is used for general conversations. 알려 줘요 (allyeo jwoyo) means 'tell' and is used when giving information. 물어봐요 (mureobwayo) means 'ask' and is used when seeking information or questions.

examples.english: My friend says a secret to me.
We speak at school every day.
The teacher tells us the homework.

pages.title: Start & finish the day in Korean
pages.titleEn: Start & finish the day in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows common Korean verbs used to describe starting and finishing your day. You can use these words to talk about waking up, going to work or scho…
pages.imageAlt: Start & finish the day in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How to start and finish your day in Korean 👇 🔴 일어나다 [ireonada] - wake up
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean verbs used to describe starting and finishing your day. You can use these words to talk about waking up, going to work or school, coming home, and going to bed. Some verbs have pairs that depend on whether you are talking about work or school. These verbs are useful for daily conversations.

examples.english: I wake up in the morning and go to work.
Students wake up in the morning and go to school.
I come home in the evening and go to bed early.

pages.title: Start / stop / continue in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows common Korean verbs used to talk about starting, stopping, and continuing actions. '시작해요' means to start something, '멈춰요' means to stop, '계속…
pages.imageAlt: Start / stop / continue in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Want to say start, stop, or continue in Korean? 🔴 시작해요 [sijakhaeyo] - start
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean verbs used to talk about starting, stopping, and continuing actions. '시작해요' means to start something, '멈춰요' means to stop, '계속해요' means to continue, and '그만해요' means to quit or stop doing something completely. These verbs are useful for everyday conversations when describing actions or activities.

examples.english: The class starts.
Let's stop for a moment.
I continue studying.

pages.title: Still / already / yet in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 아직, 벌써, 아직 안, and 더 이상 are used to talk about time and actions. 아직 means 'still' and shows that something is continuing. 벌써 means 'already' and sh…
pages.imageAlt: Still / already / yet in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How to say still, already, and yet in Korean? 🔴 아직 [ajik] - still
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 아직, 벌써, 아직 안, and 더 이상 are used to talk about time and actions. 아직 means 'still' and shows that something is continuing. 벌써 means 'already' and shows that something happened sooner than expected. 아직 안 means 'not yet' and is used to say something has not happened up to now. 더 이상 means 'anymore' and is used to say something no longer happens.

examples.english: I am still doing my homework.
He already went home.
I have not eaten yet.

pages.title: Start / stop / continue in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows common Korean verbs and expressions used to talk about starting, stopping, and continuing actions. '시작해요' means to start something, '멈춰요' me…
pages.imageAlt: Start / stop / continue in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Need to tell someone to start, stop, or continue something in Korean? Use these easy words 👇 🔴 시작해요 [sijakhaeyo] - Start
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean verbs and expressions used to talk about starting, stopping, and continuing actions. '시작해요' means to start something, '멈춰요' means to stop, and '계속해요' means to continue. '잠깐만요' is used to ask someone to pause briefly. These words help you describe actions in everyday situations clearly.

examples.english: We start the class.
Wait a moment, I have a phone call.
I continue working.

pages.title: Time words in Korean
pages.description: These Korean time words help you talk about when something happens. '지금' means 'now,' and it's used for the present moment. '아까' refers to a short time ago,…
pages.imageAlt: Time words in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Talk about time in Korean like a pro! 🕒 지금 [jigeum] - now
pages.explanationEn: These Korean time words help you talk about when something happens. '지금' means 'now,' and it's used for the present moment. '아까' refers to a short time ago, like 'a while ago.' '나중에' means 'later,' indicating a future time, and '내일' specifically means 'tomorrow.' Learning these words helps you describe time clearly in everyday conversations.

examples.english: What are you doing now?
I met a friend a while ago.
I will call you again later.

pages.title: Also / too particles in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, particles like 도 (do) and 만 (man) are used to express 'also', 'too', or 'only'. They help add meaning to nouns by showing inclusion or limitation.…
pages.imageAlt: Also / too particles in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Learn how to say "also" or "too" in Korean with these easy examples👇 🔴 나도 [nado] - me too
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, particles like 도 (do) and 만 (man) are used to express 'also', 'too', or 'only'. They help add meaning to nouns by showing inclusion or limitation. For example, 도 means 'also' or 'too', while 만 means 'only'. These particles are important for making comparisons or emphasizing specific items in a sentence.

examples.english: I also go to school.
This is delicious too.
Even I didn't know that.

pages.title: Too / enough in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, words like 너무 (too) and 충분해요 (enough) help describe the degree of something. 너무 means something is excessive or more than needed, while 충분해요 means…
pages.imageAlt: Too / enough in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How to say "too" and "enough" in Korean? 🔴 너무 [neomu] - too much
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, words like 너무 (too) and 충분해요 (enough) help describe the degree of something. 너무 means something is excessive or more than needed, while 충분해요 means there is a sufficient amount. 조금 means a small amount, and 부족해요 means not enough. These words help express whether something is too much, enough, or not enough in everyday situations.

examples.english: This food is too spicy.
There is enough time.
Please give me a little more.

pages.title: Too / only / even in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 도, 만, and 조차 are particles used to express inclusion, limitation, and emphasis respectively. 도 means 'too' or 'also' and adds information by inclu…
pages.imageAlt: Too / only / even in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for too / only / even ✨ 🔴 도 [do] - too / also
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 도, 만, and 조차 are particles used to express inclusion, limitation, and emphasis respectively. 도 means 'too' or 'also' and adds information by including something additional. 만 means 'only' and limits the scope to a specific item or group. 조차 means 'even' and emphasizes an extreme or unexpected case. These particles help clarify relationships and focus in sentences.

examples.english: I also go to school.
I only drink water.

examples.korean: 어제는 비가 와서 운동조차 못 했어요.
examples.english: It rained yesterday, so I couldn't even exercise.

pages.title: Topic vs subject particles in Korean
pages.titleEn: Topic vs subject particles in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, topic particles and subject particles are used to mark different parts of a sentence. Topic particles like '는' highlight what the sentence is abou…
pages.imageAlt: Topic vs subject particles in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Topic vs Subject particles in Korean can be tricky! 🔴 나는 [naneun] - as for me...
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, topic particles and subject particles are used to mark different parts of a sentence. Topic particles like '는' highlight what the sentence is about or what you want to talk about. Subject particles like '가' show who or what performs the action or exists in the sentence. Understanding the difference helps you make clear and natural sentences.

examples.english: As for me, I like coffee.
The coffee is delicious.
I made the coffee.

pages.title: Try doing in Korean
pages.description: The expressions in this chart are used to talk about trying something in Korean. They help you say that you will try, have tried, or encourage someone to try…
pages.imageAlt: Try doing in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for try doing ✨ 🔴 해 보다 [hae boda] - try -ing
pages.explanationEn: The expressions in this chart are used to talk about trying something in Korean. They help you say that you will try, have tried, or encourage someone to try an action. These phrases are useful for beginners to express attempts or experiences with different activities.

examples.english: Have you tried new food?
I will try it once too.
Don't worry and give it a try.

pages.title: Try it out grammar in Korean
pages.titleEn: Try it out grammar in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows different ways to express trying or doing something in Korean. '해요' means 'do it' or 'I do.' '해 봐요' is used to suggest trying something. '해…
pages.imageAlt: Try it out grammar in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for try it out grammar ✨ 🔴 해요 [haeyo] - do it
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows different ways to express trying or doing something in Korean. '해요' means 'do it' or 'I do.' '해 봐요' is used to suggest trying something. '해 봤어요?' asks if someone has tried something before. '해 볼게요' means 'I'll try' or 'I will give it a try.' These forms help you talk about actions and experiences in everyday situations.

examples.english: Try making this food.
Have you tried exercising?
Yes, I'll try!

pages.title: Try vs do in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, '해요' means 'do' and is used for regular actions. '해 봐요' means 'try' and shows an attempt to do something. When you want to encourage someone not t…
pages.imageAlt: Try vs do in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Want to say "try" vs "do" in Korean? 🔵 해요 [haeyo] - do (just do it)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, '해요' means 'do' and is used for regular actions. '해 봐요' means 'try' and shows an attempt to do something. When you want to encourage someone not to stop, you say '계속 해 봐요' which means 'keep trying.' If you give up, you say '포기해요.' These verbs help express effort and action clearly.

examples.english: I do my homework.
Try new food.
Don't give up and keep trying.

pages.title: Want / hope / wish in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows different ways to express want, hope, and wish in Korean. 싶어요 is used to say you want something or want to do something. 바라요 expresses hope…
pages.imageAlt: Want / hope / wish in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How to say want, hope, and wish in Korean? 🔴 싶어요 [sipeoyo] - want
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows different ways to express want, hope, and wish in Korean. 싶어요 is used to say you want something or want to do something. 바라요 expresses hope or a polite wish for something to happen. 했으면 좋겠어요 is a phrase to express a wish or desire for a situation to be different. 하고 싶은데요 is used when you want to do something but may have some hesitation or want to explain more.

examples.english: I want to learn Korean.
I wish the weather would be nice tomorrow.
I'd like to travel, but I don't have time.

pages.title: Want vs like in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 'want' and 'like' are expressed differently. To say you want to do something, use the verb stem plus '고 싶어요.' To say you like something, use the o…
pages.imageAlt: Want vs like in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Want vs Like in Korean can be tricky! 🔴 먹고 싶어요 [meokgo sipeoyo] - I want to eat
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 'want' and 'like' are expressed differently. To say you want to do something, use the verb stem plus '고 싶어요.' To say you like something, use the object plus '좋아해요.' This helps you talk about desires and preferences clearly.

examples.english: I want to eat.
I like noodles.
I like traveling.

pages.title: Wear / put on in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, different verbs are used to describe wearing or putting on various items. 입어요 is used for clothes, 써요 for hats or glasses, 신어요 for shoes, and 벗어요…
pages.imageAlt: Wear / put on in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How do you say "wear" or "put on" in Korean? Use these when talking about clothes and accessories 👇
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, different verbs are used to describe wearing or putting on various items. 입어요 is used for clothes, 써요 for hats or glasses, 신어요 for shoes, and 벗어요 means to take off clothing or accessories. These verbs help you talk about daily actions related to dressing.

examples.english: I wear new clothes today.
I wear a hat because the sun is strong.
I put on shoes when I go to school.

pages.title: While / during in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows common Korean connectors used to talk about time relationships between actions. '하면서' means 'while doing' and is used when two actions happe…
pages.imageAlt: While / during in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Use these to talk about time in Korean 👇 🔴 하면서 [hamyeonseo] - while doing
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean connectors used to talk about time relationships between actions. '하면서' means 'while doing' and is used when two actions happen at the same time. '동안' means 'during' and refers to the duration of an event. '하자마자' means 'as soon as' and indicates one action happens immediately after another. '하기 전에' means 'before doing' and is used to talk about an action that happens before another.

examples.english: I study while listening to music.
I traveled a lot during the summer.
As soon as I got home, I took a shower.

pages.title: With vs without in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows how to express 'with' and 'without' in Korean. Use '와/과 함께' to say 'with' when talking about companionship or doing something together. Use…
pages.imageAlt: With vs without in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for with vs without ✨ 🔴 와/과 함께 [wa/gwa hamkke] - with
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how to express 'with' and 'without' in Korean. Use '와/과 함께' to say 'with' when talking about companionship or doing something together. Use '없이' to say 'without' when something is missing or not included. Words like '혼자' and '같이' help describe being alone or together in simple sentences.

examples.english: I watched a movie with my friend.
I started my morning without coffee.

examples.korean: 혼자 공부하는 것보다 같이 공부하는 게 좋아요.
examples.english: Studying together is better than studying alone.

pages.title: Agreement glue words in Korean
pages.description: Agreement glue words in Korean are small expressions that help show agreement, confirmation, or connection in conversations. They make your speech sound natu…
pages.imageAlt: Agreement glue words in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Need quick agreement words in Korean? 🔵 그치 [geuchi] - Right?
pages.explanationEn: Agreement glue words in Korean are small expressions that help show agreement, confirmation, or connection in conversations. They make your speech sound natural and friendly when you agree with someone or want to include them. These words are often used in spoken Korean and help keep the conversation flowing smoothly.

examples.english: The weather is really nice today, right?
Let's do it together! It will be fun.
So, I decided to go with you.

pages.title: Soft apology words in Korean
pages.description: These soft apology words in Korean are polite and gentle ways to say sorry in everyday conversations. They are often used among friends or in casual situatio…
pages.imageAlt: Soft apology words in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Need soft ways to say sorry in Korean? Use these when you want to sound extra gentle 👇 🔵 미안해 [mianhae] - Sorry
pages.explanationEn: These soft apology words in Korean are polite and gentle ways to say sorry in everyday conversations. They are often used among friends or in casual situations to show sincerity without sounding too formal. Using these phrases helps maintain good relationships and shows respect. The words range from simple apologies to expressions that emphasize regret or promise not to repeat mistakes.

examples.english: Sorry, friend. I was late.

examples.korean: 진짜 미안해. 다시는 그럴 일이 없을 거야.
examples.english: I'm really sorry. It won't happen again.
I was rude. I'll be careful next time.

pages.title: Café mood words in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows common Korean words and phrases you can use in a café setting. These words express moods, tastes, and simple questions you might hear or say…
pages.imageAlt: Café mood words in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Feel the café mood in Korean ☕️💙 🔵 달달해 [daldalhae] - Sweet
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean words and phrases you can use in a café setting. These words express moods, tastes, and simple questions you might hear or say while enjoying a drink or snack. They are easy to remember and useful for everyday conversations in a café. The words include feelings like sweet and bitter, as well as polite expressions like 'How much?' and 'Goodbye.'

examples.english: This coffee is sweet. It's really delicious!

examples.korean: 저는 써서 좋아하지 않아요. 편한 자리로 갈까요?
examples.english: I don't like it because it's bitter. Shall we go to a comfortable seat?
I'm hungry. How much is this cake?

pages.title: Mini celebration words in Korean
pages.description: This chart introduces common Korean words and phrases used to celebrate and show appreciation in everyday conversations. These expressions are friendly and o…
pages.imageAlt: Mini celebration words in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for mini celebration words ✨ 🔴 축하해 [chukahae] - Congrats
pages.explanationEn: This chart introduces common Korean words and phrases used to celebrate and show appreciation in everyday conversations. These expressions are friendly and often used among friends, family, or in social settings. Learning these words helps you join in celebrations and express gratitude naturally in Korean.

examples.english: Happy birthday! Today is really the best!
Well done! You really worked hard.
Thank you, everyone! It's all thanks to you.

pages.title: Chat openers in Korean
pages.description: Chat openers in Korean are common phrases used to start conversations or get someone's attention. They range from casual greetings like '야' (Hey) to polite e…
pages.imageAlt: Chat openers in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for chat openers ✨ 🔴 야 [ya] - Hey (close)
pages.explanationEn: Chat openers in Korean are common phrases used to start conversations or get someone's attention. They range from casual greetings like '야' (Hey) to polite expressions like '저기요' (Excuse me). These phrases help you connect naturally in everyday spoken Korean, whether with friends or strangers. Using the right opener sets the tone for friendly and smooth communication.

examples.english: Hey, how have you been?
Excuse me, how much is this?
I'm sorry, I'm late.

pages.title: Comfort sounds in Korean
pages.description: Comfort sounds in Korean are simple expressions used in everyday conversations to show feelings like surprise, relief, agreement, or gratitude. These sounds…
pages.imageAlt: Comfort sounds in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Need quick comfort sounds in Korean? Use these when you want to express feelings softly 👇 🔴 아이구 [aigu] - Aww / oof
pages.explanationEn: Comfort sounds in Korean are simple expressions used in everyday conversations to show feelings like surprise, relief, agreement, or gratitude. These sounds often come from mascots or cute characters, making them fun and easy to remember. They help make spoken Korean more natural and friendly. Learning these will improve your listening and speaking skills.

examples.english: Aww, the weather is so hot today!
Phew, I'm really glad the exam is over.
Thank you! The gift is really nice.

pages.title: Home cooking words in Korean
pages.description: These are common Korean phrases used when cooking at home. They help you talk about preparing food, seasoning, cooking, and cleaning up in a casual and frien…

pages.intro: Stuck at home and want to cook something? Use these cute phrases to sound like a pro in Korean! 👩‍🍳💖 🔴 뭐 해 먹지 [mwo hae meokji] - What to cook?
pages.explanationEn: These are common Korean phrases used when cooking at home. They help you talk about preparing food, seasoning, cooking, and cleaning up in a casual and friendly way. These expressions are often used in everyday conversations, especially when cooking with family or friends. Learning them will make your home cooking experience more enjoyable and interactive.

examples.english: What should we cook? Let's chop the ingredients!

examples.korean: 간 맞춰야 해. 소금 더 넣어 줘.
examples.english: We need to season it. Please add more salt.
Don't overcook it! It's done! Now let's do the dishes.

pages.title: Soft date words in Korean
pages.description: These soft date words in Korean are casual and friendly expressions often used when talking with close friends or loved ones. They help create a warm and inv…
pages.imageAlt: Soft date words in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Cute Korean date words to sound soft and sweet 💕 🔴 보고 싶었어 [bogo sipeosseo] - Missed you
pages.explanationEn: These soft date words in Korean are casual and friendly expressions often used when talking with close friends or loved ones. They help create a warm and inviting atmosphere for making plans, expressing feelings, or apologizing gently. These phrases are common in spoken Korean and add a cute, social touch to conversations.

examples.english: I missed you! When can I see you?
Where shall we go? Let's have a drink?
I'm sorry, this time you pay for me.

pages.title: Desk stretch words in Korean
pages.description: These desk stretch words in Korean describe simple exercises you can do while working to stay healthy and relaxed. They focus on moving and stretching differ…
pages.imageAlt: Desk stretch words in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Need a quick desk stretch? Try these moves to feel better fast! 👇 🔴 스트레칭 [seuteureching] - Stretch
pages.explanationEn: These desk stretch words in Korean describe simple exercises you can do while working to stay healthy and relaxed. They focus on moving and stretching different parts of your body like your spine, neck, shoulders, and wrists. Doing these stretches helps improve posture and reduce tension during long hours at a desk.

examples.korean: 일할 때 스트레칭을 자주 하면 몸이 편안해져요.
examples.english: If you stretch often while working, your body feels more comfortable.

examples.korean: 목돌리기와 어깨돌리기는 긴장을 풀어주는 좋은 방법이에요.
examples.english: Neck rolls and shoulder rolls are good ways to relieve tension.

examples.korean: 옆으로 기울이기와 앞으로숙이기를 하면 허리가 덜 아파요.
examples.english: Side bends and forward bends help reduce back pain.

pages.title: Tiny drama bits in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows tiny drama bits in Korean, which are short and casual expressions often used in everyday conversations and dramas. These phrases include rea…
pages.imageAlt: Tiny drama bits in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 🗣️ When you're deep in K-content mode: 🔴 설마 [seolma] - No way...
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows tiny drama bits in Korean, which are short and casual expressions often used in everyday conversations and dramas. These phrases include reactions, greetings, and small talk that make speech sound natural and lively. They are perfect for learners who want to understand spoken Korean and enjoy watching dramas with cute mascots like capybaras.

pages.explanationEn: The Korean idiom '어깨를 으쓱하다' means 'to shrug.' It is used when someone raises their shoulders slightly, often to show indifference, uncertainty, or lack of knowledge. This expression is common in everyday conversations to indicate that a person does not have a clear answer or does not care much about something.

examples.english: He shrugged at the question.

examples.korean: 왜 늦었는지 물었지만, 그녀는 어깨를 으쓱했다.
examples.english: I asked why she was late, but she shrugged.

examples.korean: 결과가 좋지 않아서 모두 어깨를 으쓱했다.
examples.english: Because the result was not good, everyone shrugged.

pages.explanationEn: The Korean idiom '등을 돌리다' literally means 'to turn one's back.' It is used to describe a situation where someone stops supporting or caring about another person or thing. examples.korean: 가족이 어려울 때 서로 등을 돌리지 말아야 해요.

examples.english: I am vegan, so I eat food that has no animal products.

examples.korean: 이 샐러드는 채식 식단에 맞고 고기가 없어요.
examples.english: This salad fits a vegetarian diet and contains no meat.

examples.english: I have set up electricity and water. I will connect the gas soon too.

examples.korean: 이사 예약을 했고, 청소하기도 시작했어요. 새 집 꾸미기가 기대돼요.
examples.english: I booked the move and started cleaning. I'm excited to decorate my new home.

I withdrew cash from the ATM.
I asked the teller how to transfer money using a card.

examples.english: I go to the hospital and check in first. Then, I fill out the forms.

pages.titleEn: Go in vs Go out in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows the difference between 'go in' and 'go out' in Korean. '들어가다' means to enter or go inside a place. '나가다' means to exit or go outside from a…
pages.imageAlt: Go in vs Go out in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for go in vs go out ✨ 🔴 들어가다 [deureogada] - Go in
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the difference between 'go in' and 'go out' in Korean. '들어가다' means to enter or go inside a place. '나가다' means to exit or go outside from a place. These verbs are used to describe motion related to entering or leaving spaces.

examples.english: I go into the school.
I go out from the house.
I go into the store and buy something.

pages.title: Be / have vs Be (honorific)
pages.titleEn: Be / have vs Be (honorific) in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 있다 (itda) means 'to be' or 'to have' and is used in everyday situations. 계시다 (gyesida) is the honorific form of 있다 and is used to show respect whe…
pages.imageAlt: Be / have vs Be (honorific) in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Use these when talking about people or things 👇 🔴 있다 [itda] - to be / to have
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 있다 (itda) means 'to be' or 'to have' and is used in everyday situations. 계시다 (gyesida) is the honorific form of 있다 and is used to show respect when talking about someone else's presence or possession, especially elders or people of higher status. Both verbs express existence or possession but differ in politeness level.

examples.english: The book is on the desk.
Grandfather is at home.
I have a friend.

pages.title: Explain vs Describe
pages.description: Both '설명하다' and '묘사하다' are verbs used to share information, but they focus on different ways of communication. '설명하다' means to explain something clearly, oft…
pages.imageAlt: Explain vs Describe in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Confused between 설명하다 and 묘사하다? Use 설명하다 to explain a reason or idea. Use 묘사하다 to describe how something looks or feels.
pages.explanationEn: Both '설명하다' and '묘사하다' are verbs used to share information, but they focus on different ways of communication. '설명하다' means to explain something clearly, often with reasons or details. '묘사하다' means to describe something by showing its appearance or characteristics. Use '설명하다' when you want to make something easy to understand, and '묘사하다' when you want to paint a picture with words.

examples.english: The teacher explained the problem in detail.
I described the scenery by looking at the picture.
My friend explained and described their travel experience.

pages.title: Eye vs Snow
pages.description: In Korean, the word '눈' (nun) can mean both 'eye' and 'snow.' These two meanings sound exactly the same but are used in different contexts. Learning these ho…
pages.imageAlt: Eye vs Snow in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Look at the picture to see two meanings of 눈! 🔴 눈 [nun] - Eye
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, the word '눈' (nun) can mean both 'eye' and 'snow.' These two meanings sound exactly the same but are used in different contexts. Learning these homonyms helps you understand Korean better and avoid confusion. Pay attention to the situation to know which meaning is intended.

examples.english: My eye hurts.
It is snowing a lot today.
The eyes are pretty.

pages.title: Fast vs Urgent / rushed
pages.titleEn: Fast vs Urgent / rushed in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 빠르다 means 'fast' and describes something moving or happening quickly. 급하다 means 'urgent' or 'rushed' and is used when something needs immediate at…
pages.imageAlt: Fast vs Urgent / rushed in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Need to describe speed or urgency in Korean? 🔴 빠르다 [ppareuda] - Fast
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 빠르다 means 'fast' and describes something moving or happening quickly. 급하다 means 'urgent' or 'rushed' and is used when something needs immediate attention or action. Both words relate to speed, but 빠르다 focuses on speed itself, while 급하다 emphasizes urgency or pressure to act quickly.

examples.english: That car is really fast.
The meeting is urgent, so we have to hurry.
I like walking fast.

pages.title: Finish vs Complete
pages.description: Both '끝내다' and '완료하다' mean to finish or complete something in Korean. '끝내다' is more commonly used in everyday conversation and focuses on finishing an action…
pages.imageAlt: Finish vs Complete in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When you {끝내다} something, you finish it. When you {완료하다} something, you complete it fully.
pages.explanationEn: Both '끝내다' and '완료하다' mean to finish or complete something in Korean. '끝내다' is more commonly used in everyday conversation and focuses on finishing an action or task. '완료하다' is more formal and often used in official or written contexts to indicate that something has been fully completed. Understanding the difference helps you choose the right word depending on the situation.

examples.english: I finished all my homework.
I have completed the project.
I rested after finishing the book.

pages.title: Fix vs Repair
pages.description: Both 고치다 and 수리하다 mean to fix something in Korean, but they are used differently. 고치다 is more general and can be used for fixing small problems or mistakes.…
pages.imageAlt: Fix vs Repair in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When something breaks, do you 고치다 or 수리하다 it? 🔴 고치다 [gochida] - casual fix
pages.explanationEn: Both 고치다 and 수리하다 mean to fix something in Korean, but they are used differently. 고치다 is more general and can be used for fixing small problems or mistakes. 수리하다 is more formal and usually refers to repairing machines or devices. Knowing when to use each helps you speak more naturally.

examples.english: My computer broke, so I fixed it.
I went to repair my car.
There was a hole in my clothes, so I fixed it.

pages.title: Fun vs Interesting
pages.description: The words 재미있다 and 흥미롭다 both describe positive feelings but are used differently. 재미있다 means something is fun and enjoyable, often related to activities or e…
pages.imageAlt: Fun vs Interesting in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 😂 When your fave show is just so 재미있다 [jaemiitda] (fun) you can’t stop laughing! 🤔 When a plot twist is 흥미롭다 [heungmiropda] (interesting) and makes you think hard.
pages.explanationEn: The words 재미있다 and 흥미롭다 both describe positive feelings but are used differently. 재미있다 means something is fun and enjoyable, often related to activities or experiences that make you happy. 흥미롭다 means something is interesting and captures your attention or curiosity. Understanding these differences helps you express emotions more accurately in Korean.

examples.english: This movie is really fun.
That book is very interesting.

examples.korean: 친구들과 노는 것이 재미있고, 새로운 것을 배우는 것이 흥미로워요.
examples.english: Playing with friends is fun, and learning new things is interesting.

pages.title: Give vs Give (humble)
pages.description: In Korean, there are different words for "give" depending on the level of politeness. "주다" (juda) is the common word used in everyday situations. "드리다" (deur…
pages.imageAlt: Give vs Give (humble) in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Need to say "give" politely in Korean? 🔴 주다 [juda] - Give (to anyone)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, there are different words for "give" depending on the level of politeness. "주다" (juda) is the common word used in everyday situations. "드리다" (deurida) is the humble form used when giving something to someone of higher status or to show respect. Using the correct form helps you sound polite and respectful in Korean.

examples.english: I gave a book to my friend.
I gave a gift to the teacher.
I give flowers to my mom.

pages.title: Go vs Come
pages.description: In Korean, 가다 (gada) means 'to go,' and 오다 (oda) means 'to come.' These verbs describe movement relative to the speaker's location. Use 가다 when moving away f…
pages.imageAlt: Go vs Come in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Need to talk about moving places? 🔴 가다 [gada] - Go (move away from here)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 가다 (gada) means 'to go,' and 오다 (oda) means 'to come.' These verbs describe movement relative to the speaker's location. Use 가다 when moving away from the speaker, and 오다 when moving toward the speaker. Understanding these helps you talk about directions and travel in everyday situations.

examples.english: I go to school.
A friend comes to my house.
Where are you going tomorrow?

pages.title: Hear / listen vs Be heard
pages.titleEn: Hear / listen vs Be heard in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 듣다 means to actively hear or listen to something, showing that you are paying attention. 들리다 means that a sound is heard or can be heard, focusing…
pages.imageAlt: Hear / listen vs Be heard in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When you want to say "I hear something," use 듣다 (deutda). When something "can be heard" or "is audible," use 들리다 (deullida).
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 듣다 means to actively hear or listen to something, showing that you are paying attention. 들리다 means that a sound is heard or can be heard, focusing on the sound itself being audible. 듣다 is used when the subject is intentionally listening, while 들리다 is used when the sound reaches the ears naturally or passively.

examples.english: I am listening to music.
I can hear the sound of singing outside.
The students listen well to the teacher.

pages.title: Help vs Assist
pages.description: Both '도와주다' and '지원하다' mean to help or assist in Korean, but they are used differently. '도와주다' is more casual and common in everyday situations when helping…
pages.imageAlt: Help vs Assist in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When you want to casually help a friend, use 도와주다 [dowajuda] - Help For formal or official support, say 지원하다 [jiwonhada] - Assist
pages.explanationEn: Both '도와주다' and '지원하다' mean to help or assist in Korean, but they are used differently. '도와주다' is more casual and common in everyday situations when helping someone directly. '지원하다' is more formal and often used in official or professional contexts, like supporting a project or applying for a job.

examples.english: My friend helped me with my homework.
The company provides assistance to its employees.
I want to help with difficult tasks.

pages.title: Hide vs Conceal
pages.description: Both '숨기다' and '감추다' mean to hide something in Korean, but they are used slightly differently. '숨기다' often refers to hiding something physically or keeping i…
pages.imageAlt: Hide vs Conceal in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When you want to keep something secret, do you 숨기다 or 감추다? 🤔 🔴 숨기다 [sumgida] - Hide an object
pages.explanationEn: Both '숨기다' and '감추다' mean to hide something in Korean, but they are used slightly differently. '숨기다' often refers to hiding something physically or keeping it secret. '감추다' can also mean to conceal, but it sometimes implies hiding something more carefully or deeply. They are similar verbs used for hiding, but context can change which one fits better.

examples.english: I hid the secret from my friend.
He concealed the money inside the book.
The children hid the toys well.

pages.title: Hot vs Warm
pages.description: This chart shows the difference between 뜨겁다 and 따뜻하다, two Korean words related to temperature. 뜨겁다 means 'hot' and is used for things that are very hot to to…
pages.imageAlt: Hot vs Warm in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 🔥 When your coffee is too 뜨겁다 [tteugeopda] (hot) to drink… ☀️ When the sun feels just 따뜻하다 [ttatteuthada] (warm) on a chill day…
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the difference between 뜨겁다 and 따뜻하다, two Korean words related to temperature. 뜨겁다 means 'hot' and is used for things that are very hot to touch or taste. 따뜻하다 means 'warm' and describes a comfortable, mild heat. Understanding these helps you talk about temperature more naturally in Korean.

examples.english: This coffee is too hot.
The weather is warm, so I feel good.
My hand touched hot water.

pages.title: Hurt / sick vs Uncomfortable
pages.titleEn: Hurt / sick vs Uncomfortable in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 아프다 means to be hurt or sick, referring to physical pain or illness. 불편하다 means to feel uncomfortable, often about situations, feelings, or physic…
pages.imageAlt: Hurt / sick vs Uncomfortable in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 🗣️ When your body says no: ➡️ 아프다 [apeuda] (Hurt / sick) means pain or illness.
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 아프다 means to be hurt or sick, referring to physical pain or illness. 불편하다 means to feel uncomfortable, often about situations, feelings, or physical discomfort that is not necessarily pain. Use 아프다 when talking about pain or sickness, and 불편하다 when describing discomfort or inconvenience.

examples.english: My head hurts, so I took medicine.
This chair is very uncomfortable.
I caught a cold and my body hurts.

pages.title: Include vs Exclude
pages.description: The words 포함하다 and 제외하다 are opposites used to talk about including or excluding something in Korean. 포함하다 means to include or contain something as part of a…
pages.imageAlt: Include vs Exclude in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Confused between 포함하다 and 제외하다? 🔴 포함하다 [pohamhada] - Include
pages.explanationEn: The words 포함하다 and 제외하다 are opposites used to talk about including or excluding something in Korean. 포함하다 means to include or contain something as part of a group or list. 제외하다 means to exclude or leave something out. These words help explain what is or isn't part of a group or category.

examples.english: This price includes tax.
Students exclude drinks from their lunch.

examples.korean: 회의 참석자 명단에 나를 포함해 주세요.
examples.english: Please include me in the meeting attendee list.

pages.title: Increase vs Decrease
pages.description: This chart shows two opposite Korean verbs: 늘다 and 줄다. 늘다 means to increase or grow in number or amount, while 줄다 means to decrease or become less. These wor…
pages.imageAlt: Increase vs Decrease in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 🗣️ Real-life Korean vibes: ➡️ Increase: 늘다 [neulda] (Increase) 📈🔥
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows two opposite Korean verbs: 늘다 and 줄다. 늘다 means to increase or grow in number or amount, while 줄다 means to decrease or become less. These words are often used when talking about changes in quantity, size, or frequency. They help describe how something changes over time.

examples.korean: 우리 가게 매출이 작년에 비해 많이 늘었어요.
examples.english: Our store's sales increased a lot compared to last year.
I exercised and my weight decreased.
The number of students is gradually increasing.

pages.title: Invite vs Recommend
pages.description: Invite and recommend are two common verbs used in social situations. 초대하다 means to invite someone to an event or place, like a party or meeting. 추천하다 means t…
pages.imageAlt: Invite vs Recommend in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When you want to bring a friend to a party, use: 🔴 초대하다 [chodaehada] - Invite
pages.explanationEn: Invite and recommend are two common verbs used in social situations. 초대하다 means to invite someone to an event or place, like a party or meeting. 추천하다 means to recommend something or someone, like a restaurant or a book. Both words help you connect with others but in different ways.

examples.english: I invited my friend to the birthday party.
Please recommend a good movie.
The teacher recommended a good book.

pages.title: Kind vs Affectionate
pages.description: The words 친절하다 and 다정하다 both describe positive personality traits in Korean, but they focus on different types of warmth. 친절하다 means to be kind, showing help…
pages.imageAlt: Kind vs Affectionate in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 🗣️ When you meet a new friend: ➡️ They are 친절하다 [chinjeolhada] (Kind) if they help politely.
pages.explanationEn: The words 친절하다 and 다정하다 both describe positive personality traits in Korean, but they focus on different types of warmth. 친절하다 means to be kind, showing helpfulness and consideration to others. 다정하다 means to be affectionate, showing warmth and care in a gentle and loving way. Understanding these differences helps you describe people more accurately.

examples.english: That person always helps kindly.
My mom is affectionate, so I feel good.
I have a friend who is kind and affectionate.

pages.title: Know vs Understand
pages.description: In Korean, both 알다 and 이해하다 relate to knowing, but they are used differently. 알다 means to know facts or information, like recognizing or being aware of somet…
pages.imageAlt: Know vs Understand in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When you just 알다 (alda), you know a fact. But when you 이해하다 (ihae-hada), you truly understand it.
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, both 알다 and 이해하다 relate to knowing, but they are used differently. 알다 means to know facts or information, like recognizing or being aware of something. 이해하다 means to understand something deeply, like grasping the meaning or concept. These words help express different levels of cognition.

examples.english: I know that person.
I understood this problem.

examples.korean: 한국 문화를 알고 이해하는 것이 중요해요.
examples.english: It is important to know and understand Korean culture.

pages.title: Late vs Slow
pages.description: The words '늦다' and '느리다' both relate to time and speed but have different meanings. '늦다' means to be late or delayed, focusing on timing. '느리다' means slow, d…
pages.imageAlt: Late vs Slow in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Mixing up 늦다 and 느리다? Here’s a quick tip: 🔴 늦다 [neutda] - Late (after the time)
pages.explanationEn: The words '늦다' and '느리다' both relate to time and speed but have different meanings. '늦다' means to be late or delayed, focusing on timing. '느리다' means slow, describing speed or pace. Understanding the difference helps you talk about being late versus moving slowly.

examples.english: I was late to school.
That car is very slow.
I waited because the bus was late.

pages.title: Laugh vs Smile
pages.description: Laugh and smile are both ways to show happiness, but they are different. Laughing is louder and shows more excitement, while smiling is quieter and shows gen…
pages.imageAlt: Laugh vs Smile in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When you feel happy, how do you show it? 😂 웃다 [utda] - Laugh out loud
pages.explanationEn: Laugh and smile are both ways to show happiness, but they are different. Laughing is louder and shows more excitement, while smiling is quieter and shows gentle happiness. In Korean, 웃다 means to laugh, and 미소짓다 means to smile. Learning these words helps you express different emotions clearly.

examples.english: He laughed loudly at the joke.

examples.korean: 그녀는 사진을 찍을 때 항상 미소짓는다.
examples.english: She always smiles when taking pictures.
The children laughing and smiling look cute.

pages.title: Leave vs Depart
pages.description: Both '떠나다' and '출발하다' mean to leave or go away, but they are used differently. '떠나다' is a general term for leaving a place or situation. '출발하다' is more speci…
pages.imageAlt: Leave vs Depart in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 🛫 When you’re about to start your trip: ➡️ 떠나다 [tteonada] (Leave) means to go away from a place
pages.explanationEn: Both '떠나다' and '출발하다' mean to leave or go away, but they are used differently. '떠나다' is a general term for leaving a place or situation. '출발하다' is more specific and is used when starting a trip, journey, or moving from one place to another, often with a vehicle.

examples.english: I left the house.
The train departs at 9 o'clock.
We prepared to leave for the trip.

pages.title: Like vs Love
pages.description: In Korean, 좋아하다 (joahada) means 'to like' and 사랑하다 (saranghada) means 'to love.' 좋아하다 is used for general liking or fondness, such as liking food, hobbies, o…
pages.imageAlt: Like vs Love in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 💖 Like vs Love in K-drama feels! 🗣️ When you 좋아하다 [joahada] (like) someone:
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 좋아하다 (joahada) means 'to like' and 사랑하다 (saranghada) means 'to love.' 좋아하다 is used for general liking or fondness, such as liking food, hobbies, or people. 사랑하다 expresses a deeper, more emotional feeling, often used for romantic love or strong affection.

examples.english: I like Korean food.
I love that person.
I like music, but I love my family.

pages.title: Look vs Check
pages.description: Both '보다' and '확인하다' are verbs related to seeing or checking something in Korean. '보다' means 'to look' or 'to see' and is used when you simply observe or wat…
pages.imageAlt: Look vs Check in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 👀 When you just want to see the cool K-drama scene: ➡️ … 보다 [boda] (Look) …
pages.explanationEn: Both '보다' and '확인하다' are verbs related to seeing or checking something in Korean. '보다' means 'to look' or 'to see' and is used when you simply observe or watch something. '확인하다' means 'to check' or 'to confirm' and is used when you want to verify or make sure of something. These verbs help express different ways of using your eyes in daily situations.

examples.english: I watch the news every morning.
Please check your plane ticket again.
Look outside the window. The weather is nice.

pages.title: Look for vs Find / discover
pages.titleEn: Look for vs Find / discover in Korean

pages.title: Make vs Produce
pages.description: Both 만들다 and 제작하다 mean to create something, but 만들다 is more general and commonly used in everyday situations for making or building things. 제작하다 is more form…
pages.imageAlt: Make vs Produce in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 🗣️ When you want to say "to make" something by hand or casually: ➡️ 만들다 [mandeulda] (Make)
pages.explanationEn: Both 만들다 and 제작하다 mean to create something, but 만들다 is more general and commonly used in everyday situations for making or building things. 제작하다 is more formal and often used for producing items like movies, products, or artworks. Use 만들다 for simple making and 제작하다 for professional or official production.

examples.english: I made a cake.
This company produces cars.
The students are making robots.

pages.title: Meet vs Meet (humble)
pages.description: In Korean, there are different words for "meet" depending on the level of politeness. "만나다 (mannada)" is the standard word used in everyday situations. "뵙다 (…

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, there are different words for "meet" depending on the level of politeness. "만나다 (mannada)" is the standard word used in everyday situations. "뵙다 (boepda)" is the humble form used when speaking about meeting someone of higher status or to show respect. Understanding these helps you speak politely in different social settings.

examples.english: I meet my friend.
I will meet (humbly) the teacher.
Tomorrow, I will meet (humbly) the company president.

pages.title: Miss vs Long for
pages.titleEn: Miss vs Long for in Korean
pages.description: Both '보고 싶다' and '그리워하다' express feelings of missing someone or something in Korean. '보고 싶다' is commonly used to say you want to see or meet someone, often i…
pages.imageAlt: Miss vs Long for in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Ever felt the difference between 보고 싶다 and 그리워하다? 🗣️ When you just want to see them soon:
pages.explanationEn: Both '보고 싶다' and '그리워하다' express feelings of missing someone or something in Korean. '보고 싶다' is commonly used to say you want to see or meet someone, often in casual or everyday situations. '그리워하다' is a bit more formal and emotional, used when you deeply long for someone or something that is absent or far away.

examples.english: I really miss my friend.
I long for my hometown.
I deeply miss because we haven't met for a long time.

pages.title: Need vs Require
pages.description: Both 필요하다 and 요구하다 express the idea of needing something, but they are used differently. 필요하다 means 'to need' in a general or personal sense, like needing an…
pages.imageAlt: Need vs Require in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When you want to say you just can't live without it 🥺: ➡️ 필요하다 [piryohada] (Need)
pages.explanationEn: Both 필요하다 and 요구하다 express the idea of needing something, but they are used differently. 필요하다 means 'to need' in a general or personal sense, like needing an item or help. 요구하다 means 'to require' or 'to demand,' often used in more formal or official situations. Understanding the difference helps you use these verbs correctly in everyday and formal contexts.

examples.english: I need water.

examples.korean: 회사는 직원들에게 더 많은 노력을 요구합니다.
examples.english: The company requires more effort from the employees.
This work needs a lot of time.

pages.title: Okay / fine vs Good
pages.titleEn: Okay / fine vs Good in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 괜찮다 (gwaenchanta) and 좋다 (jota) both express positive feelings but are used differently. 괜찮다 means 'okay' or 'fine' and is often used to show some…

pages.intro: When someone asks "How are you?" and you want to say it's okay or good, what's the difference? 🔴 괜찮다 [gwaenchanta] - Okay, fine
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 괜찮다 (gwaenchanta) and 좋다 (jota) both express positive feelings but are used differently. 괜찮다 means 'okay' or 'fine' and is often used to show something is acceptable or not a problem. 좋다 means 'good' and expresses a stronger positive evaluation or preference. Understanding when to use each helps you sound more natural in everyday conversations.

examples.english: Is this food okay?
The weather is good today.
I thought that movie was fine.

pages.title: Open vs Turn on
pages.titleEn: Open vs Turn on in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 열다 (yeolda) means to open something like a door, book, or window. 켜다 (kyeoda) means to turn on devices or lights. Both verbs describe actions but…
pages.imageAlt: Open vs Turn on in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 🗣️ Real-life Korean vibes: ➡️ Open: 열다 [yeolda] (Open) 📈🔥
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 열다 (yeolda) means to open something like a door, book, or window. 켜다 (kyeoda) means to turn on devices or lights. Both verbs describe actions but are used for different objects and situations.

examples.english: Open the door.
Turn on the light.
I open the book and study.

pages.title: Open vs Unlock
pages.description: The verbs '열다' (yeolda) and '잠금 해제하다' (jamgeum haejehada) both relate to making something accessible, but they are used in different contexts. '열다' means 'to…
pages.imageAlt: Open vs Unlock in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 🗣️ Real-life Korean vibes: ➡️ Open: 열다 [yeolda] (Open) 📈🔥
pages.explanationEn: The verbs '열다' (yeolda) and '잠금 해제하다' (jamgeum haejehada) both relate to making something accessible, but they are used in different contexts. '열다' means 'to open' and is commonly used for physical objects like doors, windows, or books. '잠금 해제하다' means 'to unlock' and is used when removing a lock or security, such as unlocking a phone or a locked door.

examples.english: Open the door.
Unlock the phone.
Open the window to let in the breeze.

pages.title: Prepare vs Get ready
pages.titleEn: Prepare vs Get ready in Korean
pages.description: Both 준비하다 and 채비하다 mean to get ready or prepare in Korean, but they are used slightly differently. 준비하다 is the more common and general verb for preparing for…
pages.imageAlt: Prepare vs Get ready in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Use these when you want to be fully set for something 👇 🔴 준비하다 [junbihada] - to prepare materials
pages.explanationEn: Both 준비하다 and 채비하다 mean to get ready or prepare in Korean, but they are used slightly differently. 준비하다 is the more common and general verb for preparing for anything, like studying or cooking. 채비하다 is often used when getting physically ready, like packing or dressing, and sounds a bit more formal or old-fashioned.

examples.english: I am preparing hard for the exam.
I have finished getting ready for the trip.
I will help prepare dinner.

pages.title: Pretty vs Beautiful
pages.description: In Korean, both 예쁘다 (yeppeuda) and 아름답다 (areumdapda) describe something that looks nice, but they have different feelings. 예쁘다 means 'pretty' and is often us…
pages.imageAlt: Pretty vs Beautiful in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Pretty vs Beautiful — when to use each? 👀 🔴 예쁘다 [yeppeuda] - pretty, cute look
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, both 예쁘다 (yeppeuda) and 아름답다 (areumdapda) describe something that looks nice, but they have different feelings. 예쁘다 means 'pretty' and is often used for people, clothes, or small things that look cute or charming. 아름답다 means 'beautiful' and is used for things that are more impressive or elegant, like nature, art, or a person's deep beauty. Knowing when to use each helps you describe appearance more naturally.

examples.english: That flower is really pretty.
That mountain is beautiful.

examples.korean: 친구가 새 옷을 입어서 예뻐 보여요.
examples.english: My friend looks pretty wearing new clothes.

pages.title: Promise vs Vow
pages.description: Promise and vow both mean to say you will do something, but promise is more common and casual. A vow is a stronger, more serious commitment, often used in im…
pages.imageAlt: Promise vs Vow in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 🗣️ When you say you’ll meet your friend later: ➡️ 약속하다 [yaksokhada] (Promise) keeps it casual and friendly
pages.explanationEn: Promise and vow both mean to say you will do something, but promise is more common and casual. A vow is a stronger, more serious commitment, often used in important or formal situations. In Korean, 약속하다 is used for everyday promises, while 맹세하다 is for solemn vows.

examples.english: I promised to do my homework by tomorrow.
At the wedding, they vowed to love each other.
I promised my friend I wouldn’t be late.

pages.title: Protect vs Defend
pages.description: Both 보호하다 and 방어하다 mean to keep something safe, but they are used differently. 보호하다 means to protect by caring or guarding something gently. 방어하다 means to de…
pages.imageAlt: Protect vs Defend in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Use these when you want to stay safe or fight back 👇 🔴 보호하다 [bohohada] - Protect (keep safe)
pages.explanationEn: Both 보호하다 and 방어하다 mean to keep something safe, but they are used differently. 보호하다 means to protect by caring or guarding something gently. 방어하다 means to defend by fighting back or resisting an attack. Use 보호하다 for general protection and 방어하다 for active defense.

examples.english: The mother protects her child.
The soldier defends the country.
We must protect the environment.

pages.title: sim put damda neota
pages.titleEn: sim put damda neota in Korean

pages.intro: How do you say "put in" in Korean? 🔴 담다 [damda] - Put in a container
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, both 담다 and 넣다 mean 'to put in,' but they are used differently. 담다 is used when putting something into a container or a space that holds things, like a bowl or a bag. 넣다 is more general and can be used for putting things into places, pockets, or even abstract ideas. Understanding the difference helps you use these verbs naturally in everyday conversation.

examples.english: I put rice into the bowl.
I put the book into the bag.
I put the letter into the envelope.

pages.title: sim put in vs into

pages.intro: Struggling with 담다 vs 넣다? 🤔 🔴 담다 [damda] - Put in (container)
pages.explanationEn: Both 담다 and 넣다 mean 'to put in' in Korean, but they are used differently. 담다 is used when putting something into a container or dish, often implying careful placement. 넣다 is more general and can be used for putting things into places or objects without focusing on the container. Understanding this difference helps you choose the right verb in everyday situations.

examples.english: I put rice into the food (dish).
I put the book into the bag.
Please put water into the cup.

pages.title: Put on vs Take off
pages.titleEn: Put on vs Take off in Korean

pages.intro: Confused about 입다 vs 벗다? 🔴 입다 [ipda] - Put on (clothes)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 입다 means 'to put on' clothes or accessories, while 벗다 means 'to take off' them. These verbs are used when talking about wearing or removing items like shirts, shoes, or hats. Understanding these words helps you describe daily actions related to clothing.

examples.english: I put on new clothes this morning.
I took off my shoes when I entered the house.
Because it was cold, I put on a coat.

pages.title: Receive vs Obtain / get
pages.titleEn: Receive vs Obtain / get in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, both 받다 and 얻다 mean to get something, but they are used differently. 받다 is used when you receive something from someone, like a gift or a message.…
pages.imageAlt: Receive vs Obtain / get in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Get confused between 받다 and 얻다? Use these when you need to talk about getting things in Korean 👇 🔴 받다 [batda] - to receive something given to you
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, both 받다 and 얻다 mean to get something, but they are used differently. 받다 is used when you receive something from someone, like a gift or a message. 얻다 means to obtain or get something through effort or by finding it. Understanding the difference helps you use these words correctly in daily conversations.

examples.english: I received a book from the teacher.
I obtained information from the internet.
I got a letter from my friend.

pages.title: Remember vs Remind
pages.description: Remember and remind are related to memory but used differently. 'Remember' means you keep something in your mind without help. 'Remind' means you help someon…
pages.imageAlt: Remember vs Remind in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Confused between 기억하다 and 상기시키다? Use these when you want to recall or remind👇 🔴 기억하다 [gieokhada] - Remember (you recall)
pages.explanationEn: Remember and remind are related to memory but used differently. 'Remember' means you keep something in your mind without help. 'Remind' means you help someone else to remember something. In Korean, 기억하다 is to remember by yourself, and 상기시키다 is to remind someone else.

examples.english: I remembered the appointment yesterday.
The teacher reminded the students of the exam date.
My friend reminded me of my birthday.

pages.title: Rest vs Relax
pages.description: In Korean, 쉬다 and 휴식하다 both relate to taking a break, but they are used differently. 쉬다 means to rest, often implying stopping work or activity to recover en…
pages.imageAlt: Rest vs Relax in Korean — Korean vocab chart

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 쉬다 and 휴식하다 both relate to taking a break, but they are used differently. 쉬다 means to rest, often implying stopping work or activity to recover energy. 휴식하다 means to relax, focusing more on calming the mind and body. Understanding these differences helps you choose the right word in daily conversations.

examples.english: I rested at home after finishing work.
I relax in the park on weekends.

examples.korean: 피곤할 때는 잠깐 쉬는 게 좋아요.
examples.english: It's good to rest for a short time when you are tired.

pages.title: Return vs Give back
pages.titleEn: Return vs Give back in Korean

pages.explanationEn: Both 돌려주다 and 반환하다 mean to give something back in Korean, but they are used differently. 돌려주다 is more common in everyday conversation and means to return something to its owner. 반환하다 is more formal and often used in official or legal contexts when giving something back.

examples.english: I returned the book to my friend.
You have to give the book back to the library.
He returned the lost wallet to the police station.

pages.title: Save vs Store

pages.intro: Need to keep something safe? 🔴 저장하다 [jeojanghada] - Save (a file, data)
pages.explanationEn: Both 저장하다 and 보관하다 mean to keep something, but they are used differently. 저장하다 is used when saving digital data like files or documents. 보관하다 means to store or keep physical items safely for a period of time. Understanding the difference helps you use these verbs correctly in daily life.

examples.english: Please save the file on the computer.
Store the books in this box.
I saved the photo and sent it to my friend.

pages.title: Say vs Mention
pages.description: In Korean, both 말하다 and 언급하다 relate to speaking, but they are used differently. 말하다 means 'to say' and is used for general speaking or expressing something d…

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, both 말하다 and 언급하다 relate to speaking, but they are used differently. 말하다 means 'to say' and is used for general speaking or expressing something directly. 언급하다 means 'to mention' and is used when referring to a topic or bringing something up in conversation. Understanding the difference helps you speak more naturally.

examples.korean: 그는 오늘 아침에 학교에 간다고 말했어요.
examples.english: He said he went to school this morning.
They mentioned the new plan in the meeting.
My friend said my name.

pages.title: See vs Be seen / appear
pages.titleEn: See vs Be seen / appear in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, '보다' means 'to see' and is used when you actively look at something. '보이다' means 'to be seen' or 'to appear,' and it describes something that can…

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, '보다' means 'to see' and is used when you actively look at something. '보이다' means 'to be seen' or 'to appear,' and it describes something that can be seen or appears to someone. These verbs show the difference between actively seeing and something being visible or appearing.

examples.english: I see the mountain.
The mountain is clearly visible.
That person appears from far away.

pages.titleEn: sim see boda boepda in Korean

'보다' is the common verb for 'see' or 'meet' used in everyday situations. '뵙다' is a humble form used when speaking about meeting someone of higher status or to show respect. Understanding when to use these helps you speak politely in Korean.

examples.english: I saw my friend today.
I will meet the teacher tomorrow (humbly).
I often see my parents.

pages.imageAlt: See (plain) vs See (humble) in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Need to talk about seeing someone respectfully? 👀 🔴 보다 [boda] - See (plain)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, there are different verbs for 'see' depending on the level of politeness. '보다' (boda) is the plain form used in casual or neutral situations. '뵙다' (boepda) is the humble form used when showing respect to someone of higher status, like elders or superiors. Using the correct form helps you speak politely and appropriately in different social contexts.

examples.english: I see my friend.
I will see the teacher tomorrow.
I want to see my grandfather often.

pages.title: Send vs Deliver
pages.description: Both 보내다 and 배달하다 are verbs related to moving something from one place to another. 보내다 means 'to send' and is used when you send letters, messages, or items…
pages.imageAlt: Send vs Deliver in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Confused between 보내다 and 배달하다? Use these when you want to talk about sending vs delivering👇 🔴 보내다 [bonaeda] - Send a message or item
pages.explanationEn: Both 보내다 and 배달하다 are verbs related to moving something from one place to another. 보내다 means 'to send' and is used when you send letters, messages, or items yourself or through a service. 배달하다 means 'to deliver' and is used when someone brings food, packages, or goods directly to a location. The main difference is that 보내다 focuses on the act of sending, while 배달하다 focuses on the act of delivering to the recipient.

examples.english: I sent a letter to my friend.
I had food delivered to my house.
I sent a package and am waiting for the delivery.

pages.title: Send vs Mail / ship
pages.titleEn: Send vs Mail / ship in Korean

pages.intro: Need to get a package or letter out? 🔴 보내다 [bonaeda] - to send (general action)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 보내다 means 'to send' and is used for sending things like messages, gifts, or people. 부치다 means 'to mail' or 'to ship' and is used when sending packages or letters through postal services. Both verbs involve sending, but 보내다 is more general, while 부치다 specifically refers to mailing or shipping items.

examples.english: Send a letter to a friend.
Mail a package.
Send a photo by email.

pages.title: Small (size) vs Few (amount)
pages.description: In Korean, 작다 (jakda) and 적다 (jeokda) both describe something small, but they focus on different things. 작다 means 'small' in size, like a small object or spa…

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 작다 (jakda) and 적다 (jeokda) both describe something small, but they focus on different things. 작다 means 'small' in size, like a small object or space. 적다 means 'few' in amount or quantity, like a small number of items. Understanding the difference helps you describe size and quantity correctly.

examples.english: This room is small.
There are few apples.

examples.korean: 내 가방은 작지만 물건이 적지 않다.
examples.english: My bag is small, but it does not have few things.

pages.title: Speak / say vs Talk / chat
pages.titleEn: Speak / say vs Talk / chat in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, both 말하다 and 이야기하다 relate to speaking, but they are used differently. 말하다 means to speak or say something directly, often focusing on the content…
pages.imageAlt: Speak / say vs Talk / chat in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Use these when you want to express speech or conversation 👇 🔴 말하다 [malhada] - Speak / say
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, both 말하다 and 이야기하다 relate to speaking, but they are used differently. 말하다 means to speak or say something directly, often focusing on the content of what is said. 이야기하다 means to talk or chat, usually implying a more casual or conversational exchange. Understanding these differences helps you choose the right word in daily conversations.

examples.english: The teacher said something important.
I had a fun chat with my friend.
He did not speak about the problem.

pages.title: Speak vs Speak (honorific)
pages.description: In Korean, there are different ways to say 'speak' depending on the level of politeness. '말하다' is the standard way to say 'speak' used in casual or neutral s…

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, there are different ways to say 'speak' depending on the level of politeness. '말하다' is the standard way to say 'speak' used in casual or neutral situations. '말씀하다' is the honorific form, used to show respect when speaking about someone of higher status or older age. Understanding when to use these forms helps you communicate politely in Korean.

examples.english: I speak when talking with my friend.
Please speak to the teacher (honorific).
Grandmother spoke slowly (honorific).

pages.title: Spicy vs Hot (temp)

Understanding these helps you talk about food and temperature clearly in Korean.

examples.english: This food is too spicy.
The coffee is still hot.
I like food that is spicy and hot.

pages.title: Start vs Begin
pages.description: Both 시작하다 and 개시하다 mean to start or begin something in Korean. 시작하다 is more commonly used in everyday situations and casual speech. 개시하다 is more formal and o…

They can often be used interchangeably, but the level of formality is the main difference.

examples.english: To start the class.
To begin the meeting.
The festival starts this afternoon.

pages.title: sim start sijakhada chulbalhada

pages.intro: 🗣️ When your K-drama marathon is about to 시작하다 [sijakhada] (start) but your friend says it’s time to 출발하다 [chulbalhada] (depart) for the concert… ➡️ 시작하다 [sijakhada] (start)
pages.explanationEn: The verbs 시작하다 and 출발하다 both relate to beginning something, but they are used differently. 시작하다 means to start or begin an action, event, or process. 출발하다 specifically means to depart or leave a place, often used when traveling. Understanding the difference helps you use these words correctly in daily situations.

examples.english: The class starts at 9 a.m.
The train departs at 3 p.m.

examples.korean: 여행을 시작하기 전에 준비를 해야 해요.

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 공부하다 means to study, which is the act of learning new information or skills. 복습하다 means to review, which is going over what you have already learned to remember it better. pages.explanationEn: This chart compares two common spooky words in Korean: 유령 (ghost) and 괴물 (monster). Both are popular during Halloween and in scary stories, but they mean different things. 유령 refers to a spirit or ghost of a dead person, while 괴물 means a monster, which is usually a scary creature. Learning these words helps you talk about Halloween and scary themes in Korean.

examples.english: I dressed up as a ghost for Halloween.
They say a monster lives in the forest.
I like stories about ghosts and monsters.

pages.explanationEn: The words 선물 (seonmul) and 기념품 (ginyeompum) both relate to giving items, but they have different meanings. 선물 means a gift given to someone for special occasions like birthdays or holidays. 기념품 means a souvenir, which is something bought or kept to remember a place or event. Understanding the difference helps you use these words correctly in daily life.

examples.english: I gave a gift to my friend on their birthday.
I bought a souvenir when I went on a trip.
I prepare gifts for my family at Christmas.

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, both 재킷 (jaekit) and 코트 (koteu) refer to outerwear, but they are used for different styles and seasons. 재킷 usually means a lighter jacket, often worn in mild weather or indoors. 코트 refers to a heavier coat, suitable for colder weather, especially in fall and winter. Knowing the difference helps you choose the right word for your outfit or weather.

examples.english: Today, I wore a jacket to school.
I often wear a coat in the fall.
A jacket is light, and a coat is warmer.
